results.topic: Negishi, Tiruta-Barna, Schiopu, Lebert & Chevalier (2018), "An operational methodology for applying dynamic LCA to buildings" (Building and Environment), and the DyPLCA dynamic LCI model it relies on (Tiruta-Barna et al. 2016, J. Clean. Prod.; Pigné et al. 2020 web tool, Int J LCA). Covered: how process operation is modelled in time (process functioning and supply-demand functions, operation time, local time), the dynamic inventory equations, building life stages, renewal of components, and the assumptions and limits. The DyPLCA building implementation is taken from Negishi's 2019 thesis and Negishi et al. (2019). The earlier form of the equations is taken from Shimako's 2017 thesis.

sources.citation: Negishi K, Tiruta-Barna L, Schiopu N, Lebert A, Chevalier J (2018). An operational methodology for applying dynamic Life Cycle Assessment to buildings. Building and Environment 144: 611-621.
sources.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.buildenv.2018.09.005 (DOI and metadata checked on Crossref). Full text read from the author manuscript on HAL: https://hal.science/hal-04335238 (28 pp, line-numbered).
sources.time_variables: The paper defines no formal time variables. In words it uses: (1) the 'analysis time span', fixed in goal and scope and consistent with the system's lifetime (e.g. 50 yr for a building); (2) 'time zero' or 'present time', which 'can be placed anywhere on the timescale', so a study can be prospective, retrospective or in the present (Fig. 2 example: zero = start of construction); (3) 'periods with a predefined duration, e.g. 1 year, or 10 years (user defined values), each period being characterized by constant parameters for all processes involved in the period'; (4) foreground durations, e.g. construction 11-13 months and renovation 'several months'; (5) DyPLCA output given as a flow per unit time (e.g. kg/day) versus time.
sources.assumptions:
Read in full text. The paper contains no equations; all time modelling is delegated to the DyPLCA tool (ref. [48] = Tiruta-Barna et al. 2016). Five-step methodology (Fig. 1):
(1) Data calculation and collection: a dynamic thermal simulation (COMETH, hourly or daily steps) gives energy use. Reference-flow data are product name, quantity and service lifetime, e.g. 20 cm mineral insulation for 160 m2 with a 30-yr service life.
(2) Static model in SimaPro or other software with conventional matrix-based LCI. Life cycle stages are identified by activity. A repeated process (e.g. window glazing at construction and again at replacement or renovation) 'appears repeatedly in the life cycle system, but at different moments in time, which will be determined in step 4'.
(3) Dynamic model of the building system: a planned 'building dynamics DB' plus interface holding time-varying parameters, e.g. degradation of insulation thermal resistance over 25 yr, future electricity mix shares, occupancy profiles and regulations. These parameters modify the technology and environment matrices of the fore- and background, which 'should be recalculated to account for time-dependent scenarios'.
(4) Dynamic supply-chain model in DyPLCA, with the temporal database for ecoinvent 3.2. Foreground temporal characteristics are user-defined: construction takes 11-13 months; there is 'no time lag between the end of construction and the beginning of the building operation phase'; 'renovation of floors occurs after 50 years and takes several months'.
(5) Dynamic LCIA (climate change, human toxicity, ecotoxicity). Alternatively, classical LCIA 'by calculating the partial or total integral of the flows over time'.
Other points:
- The foreground is the building with three stages: construction, use and end of life.
- The time scale is 'gridded in order to define periods of constant characteristics'. Each period is modelled as a SubSystem in SimaPro, then the A and B matrices are exported to DyPLCA.
- Table 2 lists six key dynamic characteristics: occupant behaviour; construction products (performance degradation, replacement or refurbishment with new technology); energy equipment (renewables, loss of production capacity); energy mix; carbon uptake and emission (tree growth, carbonation, biogenic emission at end of life); end-of-life technologies (recycling, energy recovery).
- Section 2 quotes 50-100 yr building lifetimes from the literature, about 30 yr for principal components (floors, facades, roof), and a 12% increase in insulation conductivity over 25 yr. Components 'should be replaced or refurbished at their end of life using new technologies'.
sources.conditions_and_limits:
As stated by the authors:
- Dynamic LCIA models exist only for climate change and toxicity.
- French FDES/EPD data lack elementary flows, which hampers dynamic LCI.
- Building-dynamics data are lacking; the database was still to be developed.
- Uncertainty about future technologies applies to both static and dynamic LCA. The dynamic approach 'can evaluate the time limit from which the uncertainty rises'.
- Dynamic LCI adds uncertainty from process dynamics, durations and supply-chain delays; sensitivity analysis is recommended.
- The tools were 'still under development'.
- No case study or numbers are given in this paper.
sources.relevance: A building-level framework rather than an equation source. For C(T): renewal is a repeated foreground process placed at different times (step 2 then step 4), not a periodic rule. Time-dependent matrices are approximated by gridding time into periods of constant A and B, each with its own processes, i.e. piecewise-constant A(t) and B(t) built by process duplication. A static cumulative result is recovered by integrating the dynamic flows over a partial or the full time window. This matches a C(T) that is the integral of the summed flows up to T. Local times and process time functions are inherited from DyPLCA (see the Pigné et al. 2020 entry).

sources.citation: Tiruta-Barna L, Pigné Y, Navarrete Gutiérrez T, Benetto E (2016). Framework and computational tool for the consideration of time dependency in Life Cycle Inventory: proof of concept. Journal of Cleaner Production 116: 198-206.
sources.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2015.12.049 (Crossref confirms vol. 116, pp. 198-206, March 2016). The HAL record https://hal.science/hal-01886373 has no attached file; OpenAlex reports the paper as closed access. ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403.
sources.time_variables: Per the abstract: four temporal parameters per node, namely 'representative functioning period, production time, supply delay, supply frequency'. These are T, r, delta and tau in the later DyPLCA notation; see the Pigné et al. 2020 and Shimako 2017 entries.
sources.assumptions:
Abstract only, read from the HAL citation_abstract metadata. Conventional LCIs are 'static models of product systems without time dependent functioning of plants and time lags between supply and demand'. Process modelling describes production flows and interventions of each unit process. Supply modelling adds time lags on the materials exchanged between unit processes. The production and supply models are combined in life cycle networks. A graph search algorithm, implemented in a prototype web application, computes the time-resolved interventions. Results are (i) emission as a function of time for individual processes and (ii) the aggregated time function of each intervention. A test-bed case is solved 'both analytically and numerically'.

Secondary sources (Pigné 2020, read in full): the paper adopts a 'process/supply chain modeling perspective instead of an accounting point of view'. Its supplementary information argues that the convolution formulation (Beloin-Saint-Pierre et al. 2014) introduces 'an intrinsic dependence of the processes in the network, that is to say, a producer process will adapt its temporal characteristics ... following the consumer process, which is not the case in a real-life scenario'.
sources.conditions_and_limits: Not confirmed from the original: the equations, the test-bed case, its analytical solution and the supplementary-information convolution argument. I did not read the original paper or its supplementary information. The model equations given in this report come from later full-text sources that attribute them to this paper: Pigné et al. 2020 ESM1 (Fig. S1 'from Tiruta-Barna et al (2016)'), Negishi 2019 thesis Annex I and Shimako 2017 thesis Ch. II. Their typeset form in the 2016 original is unconfirmed.
sources.relevance: This is the origin of the DyPLCA process plus supply-chain time model that Negishi et al. (2018) apply to buildings. It is the conceptual alternative to the convolution approach: each producer keeps its own functioning profile and is placed in time by delay and supply-period parameters, rather than having its profile convolved with the consumer's.

sources.citation: Pigné Y, Navarrete Gutiérrez T, Gibon T, Schaubroeck T, Popovici E, Shimako AH, Benetto E, Tiruta-Barna L (2020). A tool to operationalize dynamic LCA, including time differentiation on the complete background database. International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment 25(2): 267-279 (online 5 Nov 2019). Includes Electronic Supplementary Material 1 (SI1).
sources.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11367-019-01696-6 (open access, CC BY 4.0). SI1 read from https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1007%2Fs11367-019-01696-6/MediaObjects/11367_2019_1696_MOESM1_ESM.docx ; HAL: hal-02353921.

equations.expression: s = A^{-1} f   (SI1 eq. 1);   g = B s   (SI1 eq. 2)
equations.symbols: A: technology matrix; a_ij = output of product i per unit of process j. A is square after allocation and is also the adjacency matrix of the process network. f: final-demand vector (reference unit). s: scaling vector, i.e. the total output of each process needed directly and indirectly for f. B: intervention matrix; b_kj = intervention k per unit of process j. g: static LCI vector.
equations.meaning: The conventional static LCI. DyPLCA keeps it 'at the level of total balances' and uses s for scaling and validation.

equations.expression: a_{i,i} = int_{t0}^{t0+T} alpha_{i,i}(t) dt   (SI1 eq. 3);   b_{k,i} = int_{t0}^{t0+T} beta_{k,i,i}(t) dt   (SI1 eq. 4)
equations.symbols: alpha_{i,i}(t): production function of process i (reference unit per time, e.g. kg/h; Table S3 gives unit/year). beta_{k,i,i}(t): intervention function of substance k for process i (e.g. kg/yr). T: representative period = lifetime of the main infrastructure supporting the activity. t0: start date.
equations.meaning: The functions are 'normalized': integrated over T they give the static coefficients. The static coefficient is therefore the process's operation spread over its infrastructure lifetime. Database rule: alpha and beta are defined over the production period r and 'replicated identically for all periods r covering the T lifetime' (T is a multiple of r).

equations.expression: sigma_{2,1} = max( floor( span_1 / tau_{2,1} ), 1 ), sigma_{2,1} >= 1 an integer   (SI1 eq. 5)
equations.symbols: sigma_{2,1}: number of batches of product 2 delivered by process 2 to process 1. span_1: functioning period of consumer 1. span_uf = T_uf for the functional-unit process, and spans are computed going upstream through the graph. tau_{2,1}: supply period (interval between two consecutive supplies).
equations.meaning: Number of supply batches over the consumer's operating time.

equations.symbols: span_2: functioning duration of producer 2. r_2: production period of process 2, i.e. the time between its earliest input and latest output.
equations.meaning: The producer's operating time is derived from the consumer's demand and propagated upstream. The Negishi 2019 thesis Annex I prints the left-hand side as span_1, which looks like a typo.

equations.symbols: alpha_{2,1}, beta_{k,2,1}: production and intervention functions of process 2 working for process 1. s_1: scaling-vector element of process 1. a_{2,1}: element of A, negative for an input. C_2: capacity factor.
equations.meaning: The producer keeps its own normalised profile (alpha_{2,2}, beta_{k,2,2}) and is rescaled so that it delivers s_1 |a_{2,1}| to the consumer.

equations.expression: Intermittent supply: C_2(t) = sigma_{2,1} int_{t}^{t+r_2} alpha_{2,2}(t) dt   (SI1 eq. 9);   continuous supply: C_2 = a_{2,2} span_1 / T_2   (SI1 eq. 10)
equations.symbols: T_2: representative period of process 2. a_{2,2}: diagonal element of A.
equations.meaning: Normalisation. With an r-periodic alpha_{2,2}, the sigma windows of length r_2 together integrate to s_1 |a_{2,1}|. (This is my arithmetic check on eqs. 7, 9 and 11, not a statement by the authors.)

equations.symbols: t_{0,1}: zero time, i.e. the start of the activity, of consumer 1. delta_2: supply delay ('no activity takes place; delay introduced for each delivered batch'; in years, Table S4). x_{2,1}: batch index.
equations.meaning: Positions each production batch of the producer in absolute time. Batch x is produced during the r_2 interval that ends delta_2 before delivery time t_{0,1} + (x-1) tau_{2,1}. This is the model's 'local time' mechanism: each process carries its own origin, shifted from its consumer's origin by -(r + delta).

equations.expression: Continuous supply: t in [ t_{0,1} - r_2 - delta_2 ,  t_{0,1} - r_2 - delta_2 + span_1 + r_2 ]   (SI1 eq. 12)
equations.symbols: As above.
equations.meaning: Continuous supply is treated as consecutive batches without pause, i.e. tau_{2,1} = r_2. My arithmetic check: for a constant alpha_{2,2}, the eq. 12 window has length span_1 + r_2 while eq. 10 normalises by span_1, so the delivered total is s_1|a_{2,1}|(1 + r_2/span_1). It is therefore exact only when r_2 is much smaller than span_1. This is not discussed by the authors.

equations.expression: g_{k,i,j} = int_{t_{0,i}}^{t_{0,f}+T_f} beta_{k,i,j}(t) dt   (SI1 eq. 13);   g_k = sum_{i=1}^{m} sum_{j=1}^{m} g_{k,i,j}   (SI1 eq. 14);   gamma_k(t) = sum_i sum_j beta_{k,i,j}(t)   (SI1 eq. 15)
equations.symbols: g_{k,i,j}: quantity of k emitted by process i working for process j. t_{0,i}: initial time and t_{0,f}+T_f: final time, as printed. m: number of processes. gamma_k(t): aggregated emission profile of substance k over the life cycle.
equations.meaning: Time integration recovers the static LCI. Eq. 14 is used for validation against g = B A^{-1} f. gamma_k(t) is the life-cycle time function that feeds dynamic LCIA.

equations.expression: Search stop rule (main text, in words): stop 'if a product exchange between two processes is lower than the product of the threshold and the process total output from the scaling vector (a_{i,j} s_j)'; also stop for activities 'starting earlier than' the time-limit date.
equations.symbols: threshold: a value between 0 and 1. Table S2 defines it as the 'minimum acceptable ratio between the quantity of material demanded by one activity and the total material quantity provided by a producer (to all consumers, over the whole life cycle ... static LCI)'. time limit: the maximum number of years the search can go back.
equations.meaning: Truncates the infinite upstream loops that matrix inversion handles implicitly. Coverage is incomplete: with threshold 1e-4, 79% of CO2 was covered in the EV case. 90% coverage would take over 5 h and 95% almost 9 days of computing.

equations.expression: Number of output time steps = (span of the time horizon + T of the FU) / step size   (SI1, in words)
equations.symbols: step size: discretisation increment of the output series. numerical precision: integration increment for the alpha integrals over r, which should be 'orders of magnitude lower than r'.
equations.meaning: Gives the discrete-time size of the 'betas' CSV output.

equations.expression: Discounting, printed as: 'the impact diminishes over time with a factor 1/(1+year)x'; Table 1 uses r = 0% and 3% over a 100-yr window
equations.symbols: x: annual discount rate; year: time in years.
equations.meaning: Optional discounting of time-resolved impacts before summing them into a single score. The printed exponent placement looks garbled. The usual form 1/(1+x)^year is not confirmed in this paper.

sources.time_variables: t: absolute timeline, anchored to the start date of the FU and built backward from FU delivery. t0 and t_{0,i}: start of the analysis or activity of each process. r: production period. T: representative period (infrastructure lifetime). span: operating duration induced by demand (span_uf = T_uf). delta: supply delay or storage. tau: supply period. sigma: number of batches. Numerical controls: time limit (yr back), threshold, numerical precision and step size. Calendar-dependent alpha is defined over 1 year starting in January. Notation warning: DyPLCA's tau is a supply interval, not a local time.
sources.assumptions:
Read in full: the paper and the SI1 docx; equations were extracted from the Word math objects.
Model and database:
- Linear static A and B are kept, and time enters only through alpha, beta, r, T, delta and tau.
- One alpha and one beta per activity in the database, applied to all of its inputs, outputs and interventions. The framework allows per-flow functions.
- Supply parameters are attributed to the producer, not to each producer-consumer pair.
- There are three supply profiles. Continuous: tau = r of the producer. Intermittent: tau = T of the consumer if supplied once per lifetime (infrastructure); tau = delta for storable frequent consumables; tau = r of the producer for seasonal supply; tau = r of the consumer for per-batch supply. Services start with or after the consumer's t0.
- Market processes are instantaneous and have no temporal parameters.
- Table S7 rules for 'Construction of buildings, infrastructures': T is the construction time; r is 'one or several years' (e.g. 10 yr for a nuclear plant); alpha is a yearly stepwise function, higher mid-year; delta is 'several tens of days'; tau = T of the consumer (single supply).
- Industrial processes: T is about 30-50 yr; r is about 1 day or several days; delta is 0 or tens of days (often 60). Maintenance: tau = 1 yr.
Algorithm:
- A search step resolves the start date and quantity of each activity, then a distribution step generates the time series.
- Workflow: model in SimaPro or OpenLCA, export A and B, then the DyPLCA temporal DB (about 15,000 ecoinvent 3.2 processes) assigns background parameters. The user sets foreground parameters.
- Outputs: a beta (per process and substance) CSV and gamma (per substance) series.
sources.conditions_and_limits:
As stated by the authors:
- Search truncation means the dynamic totals fall short of the Leontief static totals.
- The time limit can drop long-lived processes, e.g. hardwood growth with production functions defined over 140 yr.
- The same beta shape is used for all interventions of a process.
- Aggregated processes are not sequenced. Transport is an input alongside the transported good, although in reality production precedes transport. Storage is lumped into production (e.g. crop storage).
- Freight-transport durations are averages (tkm hides the duration).
- Process inventories do not change over time: 'the electricity mix has changed over time ... this issue is outside the scope'. Scenarios with different processes per period are possible but only 'in a reduced number and for a few processes'.
- Only a regular intermittent supply is implemented; a non-constant tau is future work.
- The placement of t0 under attributional versus consequential LCA is unresolved.
- The temporal database is under IP protection.
Tool availability, my own check on 2026-11-14: dyplca.univ-lehavre.fr returned HTTP 503 and dyplca.pigne.org did not respond.
sources.relevance: This is the core equation set for the dynamic LCI. In your notation: process time function e_i(t) corresponds to beta_{k,i,j}(t), or to sum_k CF_k beta_{k,i,j} for a single indicator. Local time tau_i = t - t_{i0} corresponds to t - t_{0,i}, with t_{0,producer} = t_{0,consumer} - r - delta (+ (x-1) tau for batch x). Inter-process coupling is not convolution but a batch/pulse-train supply model. My own reading, not the authors' wording: eq. 11 is equivalent to convolving the producer's one-batch profile with a delayed Dirac pulse train phi_{2,1}(t), amplitude-scaled by s_1 a_{2,1}/C_2. The producer's own shape is preserved, whereas a convolution of the producer's and consumer's distributions would smear the producer over the consumer's profile, which the authors reject. Time-dependent matrices are not native: A and B are constant per process, and time-varying technology requires period-specific duplicate processes. Cumulative C(T) = int_{start}^{T} sum_k CF_k gamma_k(t) dt; it tends to the static result as T covers everything, up to truncation.

sources.citation: Negishi K (2019). Development of a methodology of Dynamic LCA applied to the buildings (Développement d'une méthodologie d'ACV dynamique appliquée aux bâtiments). PhD thesis, INSA de Toulouse.

equations.expression: 'Product | Year Y' cursor process: delta = -Y + r (as printed); worked example 'replacement ... taking one year and ... occurs at 30 years ... Year 30 has delta = -31'. 'Year 0' processes: delta = 0 and they occur in year [-1, 0].
equations.symbols: Y: year of the maintenance or replacement event, with time zero = start of building use. r: production period of the cursor process (1 yr). delta: supply delay of the cursor process relative to its consumer. The sign is negative to place a producer later than its consumer.
equations.meaning: How renewal events are placed on the timeline. My consistency check against Fig. 4-6 and SI1 eq. 11: the producer window is [t0 - r - delta, t0 - delta], so delta = -31 with r = 1 gives [30, 31]. The rule consistent with the example is therefore delta = -(Y + r). The printed '-Y + r' would give -29, so it appears to be a typo.

equations.expression: Fig. 4-6: process 2 occupies [ t_0 - r_2 - delta_21 ,  t_0 - delta_21 ], with T_1 = r_1, T_2 = r_2 and delta_21 < 0
equations.symbols: t_0: start of process 1, the functional unit. delta_21: delay on link 2 to 1.
equations.meaning: Two-process illustration of local-time placement used for the building foreground.

equations.expression: Building process: T = r = 50 yr. Maintenance, replacement and refurbishment cursor processes: T = r = 1 and alpha = 1/T ('a constant and unitary value divided by T'). Single supply: tau = T_c.
equations.symbols: T_c: representative period of the consumer process.
equations.meaning: Foreground temporal parameterisation of building activities.

equations.expression: Degradation rules (Table 4-6, verbal, relative to the preceding year): heat-transfer coefficient of insulation +0.5%/yr; electric convector efficiency -1%/yr; heat-pump COP -3%/yr. Fig. 4-7 shows the equipment replaced every decade.
equations.symbols: Annual (yearly time step) performance values used in the COMETH dynamic thermal simulation.
equations.meaning: Year-by-year operational energy variation enters the LCI through the simulated annual energy use, not through DyPLCA functions. Written as a recurrence this is X(n) = X(n-1)(1 +/- rate); that form is my transcription of the verbal rule.

equations.expression: IRF_k(t) = a_0 + sum_{i=1}^{3} a_i exp(-t/tau_k)   (Eq. 2-1, as printed);   uRF_k = A_k IRF_k(t)   (Eq. 2-2);   RF_k(t) = int_{t0}^{t} A_k g_k(t') IRF_k(t - t') dt'   (Eq. 2-3)
equations.symbols: a_i: IRF parameters. tau_k: printed as 'lifetime of a substance i'; the index notation is ambiguous. A_k: radiative efficiency (W m-2 kg-1). g_k(t): temporal emission scenario of k, taken from the DyPLCA gamma matrix.
equations.meaning: Dynamic LCIA. Here convolution appears, between the time-resolved inventory and the atmospheric decay.

equations.expression: IRF_T = sum_n (f_n/d_n) exp(-t/d_n)   (Eq. 2-4);   AGTP_k(TH) = int_0^{TH} RF_k(t) IRF_T(TH - t) dt   (Eq. 2-5);   GMTC_k(t) = int_{t0}^{t} ( int_{t0}^{t'} A_k g_k(u) IRF_k(t' - u) du ) IRF_T(t - t') dt'   (Eq. 2-6; the printed version reuses t as the inner dummy variable, renamed u here)
equations.symbols: f_n: climate-sensitivity parameters (K (W m-2)^-1). d_n: response times (yr). TH: time horizon.
equations.meaning: Temperature response as a double convolution. Cumulative radiative forcing (CRF) is RF integrated over time. No characterisation factors or fixed horizon are needed.

sources.time_variables: Time zero = start of building use (case study 2015). Construction is [-1, 0]. Use is [0, 50]. End of life is [50, 51]. Tree growth is placed more than 100 yr before construction. Per-process r, T, delta and tau as in DyPLCA. Annual steps for degradation and energy. Electricity-mix periods are 2015-2034, 2035-2049 and 2050-2065.
sources.assumptions:
Read in full text for sections 2.2.5, 2.3.3-2.3.4, 3.2.3, 3.4, 4.3-4.4.5 and Annex I; other chapters not read.
Model description:
- Annex I restates the DyPLCA LCI equations (1)-(15), identical in substance to Pigné SI1. It says the model 'preserves this formalism ... at the level of total balances, but the connected processes are shifted in time'.
- Outputs are a Beta matrix, a Gamma matrix, and a Matrix H of totals by process for checking against g = B A^{-1} f.
Case study (3 attached wooden houses, 414 m2, 50 yr):
- Foreground graph (Fig. 4-5): Building, then 10 E+C- product families, then 'Product | Entire lifecycle', then 'Product | Year 0 / Year 0~50 / Year 50' cursor processes, then life-cycle stage modules (A1-A3, A4-A5, B1-B7, C1-C4), then ecoinvent background.
- Cursor and aggregator processes carry no interventions and act as 'the cursor on the timeline for placing real activities at the desired point in time'. Aggregators have delta = 0.
- Table 4-4 occurrence times: A1-A3 for construction at t < -1; A1-A3 for maintenance and replacement in [0, 50]; A4-A5 construction in [-1, 0] (1 yr, with energy and water); B1 use in [0, 50]; B2 maintenance (wall painting); B4 replacement (windows, doors, HVAC); B6 energy and B7 water in [0, 50]; C1-C4 for replaced products in [0, 50]; building end of life in [50, 51].
- Baseline energy: the COMETH annual consumption was 'replicated 50 times'. Future electricity mixes are new processes for 2015-2034, 2035-2049 and 2050-2065 (ADEME 2035/2050 scenarios). They are applied only to end-use energy; background processes use the current mix.
- Technological progress: windows go from 30% to 50% cullet; selected aluminium, steel and concrete fabrication processes get 10% less energy each decade; recycling rates change.
- Occupancy: 15 occupants from 2015 to 2035, then 6 adults from 2035 to 2065. Equivalent-adult formulas follow the French thermal regulation RT2012 (Eqs. 4-1 and 4-2).
- Biogenic CO2 uptake and carbonation are placed in time.
Section 3.4: construction durations from French statistics are 11-13 months for individual houses and 16-23 months for collective buildings.
sources.conditions_and_limits:
As stated by the author:
- Future mixes reuse ecoinvent 3.2 technologies.
- The mix is an annual average.
- Prospective changes cover only a few processes, because the case had more than 10,000 processes and 300,000 supplies.
- Public data on construction, renovation and demolition schedules are scarce.
- About 15 of the 63 products were cut off by the 1% criteria.
My own notes:
- The printed Annex I eq. 6 and the delta formula appear to contain typos (see the equations above).
- How the degraded, year-specific energy values (as opposed to the replicated baseline) were encoded in DyPLCA processes is not stated explicitly in the sections I read.
- The r values of the aggregator processes ('Entire lifecycle', families) are not reported. The placement arithmetic implies their t0 is effectively 0.
sources.relevance: This is the only source found that shows exactly how a building's renewal events are encoded in DyPLCA. Renewal is not generated by a service-life rule. Each event is an explicit foreground 'Year Y' process (T = r = 1, alpha = 1/T, tau = T_c, delta set to place it in [Y, Y+1]), and replaced items go to end of life at the same time. This maps directly onto your 'events at renewal times' term: each renewal gets its own local time, starting at t_{0} = Y, and its upstream fabrication is shifted earlier by r + delta. Use-stage 'year cells' are annual energy blocks (replicated, or taken from the thermal simulation). The end-of-life residual is a process placed at [50, 51]. Climate LCIA is where convolution enters.

sources.citation: Negishi K, Lebert A, Almeida D, Chevalier J, Tiruta-Barna L (2019). Evaluating climate change pathways through a building's lifecycle based on Dynamic Life Cycle Assessment. Building and Environment 164: 106377 (16 pp).
sources.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.buildenv.2019.106377 (from the HAL record; Crossref lookup failed at query time, so volume and article number are taken from HAL and the DOI). Full text: https://hal.science/hal-02311410 (author manuscript, CC BY-NC 4.0).
sources.time_variables: Year 0 = start of occupancy = 2015. The building life is 50 yr (2015-2065). The inventory timespan runs from -150 yr (tree growth) to 51 yr. The LCIA timespan runs from -150 to 500 yr. Results are reported at 100 yr and at 55 yr.
sources.assumptions:
Read in full text for sections 1-2.4; results only skimmed. This is the journal version of thesis Chapter 4, with the same five-step framework and DyPLCA parameters given in SI Table SI4.
- Table 2 matches thesis Table 4-4. It specifies that A1-A3 for replacement happens 'just before the replacement/maintenance time t' and that each product is replaced at a given t, 0 < t < 50.
- PVC window frames are replaced at 30 yr (100% landfill) and disposed of at 50 yr (92.1% landfill, 7.9% recycling). Insulation is replaced at 30 yr.
- Hourly COMETH simulation is summed to annual values: 36.9 kWh m-2 yr-1 in the first year, plus 20 kWh m-2 yr-1 for appliances.
- Scenarios vary one parameter at a time (best and worst).
- Carbonation after demolition was not included.
- The foreground is grouped by EN 15978 contributor (construction products, operational energy, operational water, on-site construction).
sources.conditions_and_limits:
As stated by the authors:
- Direct use-stage emissions from materials (VOCs, leaching) are excluded for lack of data.
- Future mixes are applied only to end-use energy; the background uses the current mix.
- Mix technologies are unchanged.
- Cut-off criteria are 1% of GWP and 1% of mass.
- The supplementary tables (SI4, SI10, SI11) were not read by me.
sources.relevance: This is the peer-reviewed case study confirming the building-stage timeline and the renewal encoding used with DyPLCA. It gives concrete windows (inventory -150 to 51 yr, LCIA up to 500 yr) relevant to choosing the study period T and the horizon of C(T).

sources.citation: Shimako AH (2017). Contribution to the development of a dynamic Life Cycle Assessment method. PhD thesis, INSA de Toulouse.

equations.expression: t_0^{l+1} = t_0^{l} - r - delta   (Eq. II.3)
equations.symbols: l: level on the supply chain. t_0^l: start date of the activity at level l. r: production period. delta: lag (delay) period.
equations.meaning: Explicit recursion for each process's own time origin. 'Every activity in the process flow presents its own start date (t0)'. This is the key parameter for distributing interventions in time.

equations.expression: a_{l+1,l} = int_{t0}^{t0+T} phi_{l+1,l}(t) dt   (Eq. II.4)
equations.symbols: phi_{l+1,l}(t): supply function (continuous or intermittent) from process l+1 to process l.
equations.meaning: The non-diagonal A coefficient is the time integral of the supply function.

equations.expression: alpha_{l+1,l}(t) = - ( s_l a_{l+1,l} / C_{l+1} ) alpha_{l+1,l+1}(t)   (Eq. II.5; printed with a trailing 'dt');   beta_{s,l+1,l}(t) = - ( s_l a_{l+1,l} / C_{l+1} ) beta_{s,l+1,l+1}(t)   (Eq. II.6)
equations.symbols: s_l: scaling element. s (subscript of beta): substance.
equations.meaning: The same scaling as Pigné SI1 eqs. 7-8.

equations.expression: C_{l+1} = ( T_l / tau_{l+1,l} ) int_{t}^{t+r_{l+1}} alpha_{l+1,l+1}(t) dt   (Eq. II.7)
equations.symbols: T_l: representative period of the consumer. tau_{l+1,l}: supply period.
equations.meaning: Earlier form of the capacity factor. Here T_l/tau plays the role later taken by the integer batch count sigma = max(floor(span/tau), 1) in Pigné SI1 eq. 9.

equations.expression: g_{s,l+1,l} = int_{t0i}^{t0f+Tf} beta_{s,l+1,l}(t) dt   (Eq. II.8)
equations.symbols: t0i: initial time; t0f+Tf: final time.
equations.meaning: Time integral recovering the static inventory.

sources.time_variables: Supply-chain level l. Start dates t_0^l. r, T, delta and tau as in DyPLCA.
sources.assumptions: Read in full text for Ch. II.2-II.3 only. The thesis recalls the model 'presented in Tiruta-Barna et al. (2016)'. A 'breadth first search' is used to place processes on the time scale. Table II.1 states 'tau = T for continuous supply'.
sources.conditions_and_limits: Pigné SI1 instead sets continuous tau = r of the producer, and its capacity factor uses sigma rather than T_l/tau. The model was revised between versions. Shimako writes the database work was done for 'more than 12 thousands activities' of ecoinvent 3.2. A mass-flow threshold and a backward time limit are imposed.
sources.relevance: This is the earliest full-text statement of the equations found, closest in time to the closed-access 2016 paper. It gives the explicit start-time recursion t_0^{l+1} = t_0^l - r - delta, which is exactly the 'local time origin' t_{i0} of your e_i(tau_i) formulation.

results.synthesis:
Sources read. In full text: Negishi et al. 2018 (HAL author manuscript); Pigné et al. 2020 with its SI1 (open access); Negishi's 2019 PhD thesis (sections listed in its entry); Negishi et al. 2019 (Building and Environment); Shimako's 2017 PhD thesis (Ch. II). Abstract only: Tiruta-Barna et al. 2016, which is closed access and has no HAL file. Its equations are known here only through those later sources, which attribute them to it.

1) What Negishi et al. (2018) contribute. A five-step workflow, with no equations:
- dynamic thermal simulation and building data;
- a static SimaPro model in which a repeated item, such as glazing at construction and at replacement, appears as separate processes;
- a planned 'building dynamics DB' of time-varying parameters that rewrite the A and B matrices;
- DyPLCA temporalisation of all supply chains;
- dynamic LCIA (climate change, toxicity), or static characterisation factors applied to 'partial or total integral of the flows over time'.
Time-varying technology, occupancy and energy mix are handled by gridding time into user-defined periods (e.g. 1 or 10 yr) of constant parameters. Each period is a SubSystem with its own processes. Time-dependent matrices are therefore piecewise constant and built by process duplication. DyPLCA itself never varies A or B in time.

2) How process operation is modelled in time (DyPLCA; Pigné SI1 eqs. 1-15, Shimako Eqs. II.1-II.8).
- Process model. Each unit process i has a production function alpha_{i,i}(t) and intervention functions beta_{k,i,i}(t). They are normalised so that their integrals over the representative period T (the infrastructure lifetime) equal the static coefficients a_{i,i} and b_{k,i}. They are defined on the production period r and repeated cyclically over T.
- Supply model, per producer-consumer link: a delay delta (storage, no activity), a supply period tau, and a continuous or intermittent mode. The supply function phi_{2,1}(t) is a pulse train.
- Operation time. The consumer's operating span (span_uf = T_uf for the functional unit) sets the number of batches, sigma = max(floor(span/tau), 1). This in turn sets the producer's span, span_2 = tau(sigma - 1) + r_2, which is propagated upstream.
- Local time. Each process has its own origin. Shimako's recursion is t_0^{l+1} = t_0^l - r - delta. Batch x of a producer occupies [t_{0,1} - r_2 - delta_2 + (x-1)tau, ... + r_2].
- Amplitude. The rescaling factor s_1 a_{2,1}/C_2 makes the delivered total equal s_1|a_{2,1}|.
- Outputs. beta_{k,i,j}(t) per substance and link; gamma_k(t) = sum over i, j of beta_{k,i,j}(t); time integrals reproduce g = B A^{-1} f, minus truncation from the threshold and the time limit.
- Coupling between processes is deliberately not a convolution of process distributions. The authors argue that convolution makes a producer adopt the consumer's temporal profile. In my reading, eq. 11 still amounts to the producer's own one-batch profile convolved with a delayed Dirac pulse train. Convolution proper appears only in the LCIA step: RF_k(t) = int A_k g_k(t') IRF_k(t - t') dt', and GMTC as a double convolution with IRF_T.

3) Building life stages and renewal (Negishi thesis Table 4-4; Negishi et al. 2019 Table 2).
- Time zero is the start of use (2015).
- Product fabrication (A1-A3) for construction occurs at t < -1. Construction (A4-A5) occupies [-1, 0]. Use (B1, B6 energy, B7 water) covers [0, 50].
- Maintenance (B2, e.g. painting) and replacement (B4: windows, doors, HVAC) occur at user-chosen years. Fabrication of the replacement items happens 'just before' that year, and replaced items go to end of life (C1-C4) at the same time.
- Building end of life occupies [50, 51]. The inventory window is -150 to 51 yr, to include tree growth. Climate indicators run to 500 yr.
- Foreground structure: the Building process (T = r = 50) is fed by family aggregators, then 'Product | Entire lifecycle', then 'Product | Year Y' cursor processes. The cursor processes have no emissions, T = r = 1, alpha = 1/T and tau = T_consumer. Their delta is chosen so that the event falls in [Y, Y+1]. The worked example (Y = 30, delta = -31) is consistent with delta = -(Y + r), not with the printed '-Y + r'.
- Renewal is thus a list of explicit, user-placed events, e.g. windows and insulation at 30 yr. It is not generated from a service-life rule.
- My own derivation from eq. 5, not stated by the authors. If renewal were generated through intermittent supply with tau = service life, sigma = max(floor(span/tau), 1) would give floor(50/30) = 1 delivery and drop the year-30 replacement. EN 15978-style counting would instead give a ceiling-based number of installations. The two differ whenever span/tau is not an integer.
- Use-stage energy is a sequence of annual blocks: COMETH annual values replicated 50 times, or year-specific values carrying insulation degradation (U +0.5%/yr), convector efficiency (-1%/yr) and heat-pump COP (-3%/yr), with equipment replaced every decade.
- The electricity mix changes only in three periods, through separate mix processes, and only for end-use energy.

4) Mapping to the C(T) to e_i(t) extension (my interpretation).
- Constants (construction) become processes placed in [-1, 0] with single supply. Their upstream fabrication is shifted earlier by r + delta.
- Year cells become annual operational processes over [0, 50].
- Renewal events become 'Year Y' processes with their own local time tau_i = t - Y.
- The end-of-life residual becomes a process in [50, 51].
- C(T) = int_{start}^{T} sum_k CF_k gamma_k(t) dt with static characterisation factors, matching Negishi's 'partial integral'. Alternatively C(T) is a dynamic indicator such as CRF(T).
- Notation clash: DyPLCA's tau is the supply period, not a local time.
- DyPLCA's 'time-dependent matrices' are time-invariant A and B plus time functions and offsets, with period-specific process copies for technology or mix change. This is not a continuous A(t).

5) Assumptions and limits.
- Linearity and static per-process coefficients.
- One beta shape per process.
- Supply parameters attached to the producer.
- No sequencing inside aggregated processes; transport and storage are lumped.
- Regular intermittent supply only.
- Truncated graph search: 79% CO2 coverage at threshold 1e-4 in the EV case.
- The time limit can drop processes with very long production functions.
- Integration precision must be much smaller than r.
- Dynamic LCIA exists only for climate and toxicity.
- Building-dynamics data are scarce.
- On my check of 14 Nov 2026, the web tool did not respond: one URL returned HTTP 503 and the other gave no response.
- Inconsistencies between versions:
  - continuous tau = T (Shimako) versus tau = r (Pigné);
  - capacity factor T_l/tau versus sigma;
  - the left-hand side of thesis eq. 6;
  - the delta formula typo;
  - the garbled discount expression;
  - my derived observation that the continuous-supply normalisation is off by a factor (1 + r_2/span_1).
results.open_questions:
1) The original Tiruta-Barna et al. (2016) paper and its supplementary information (closed access) were not read. Still to check against them: the exact original equations, the analytical solution of the test bed, and the argument against convolution. A library copy is needed.
2) Is the continuous-supply normalisation exact as implemented (eq. 10 against the eq. 12 window length span_1 + r_2)? Is span_2 for continuous supply defined as span_1 + r_2? Neither is stated.
3) How did Negishi encode year-specific degraded energy demand in DyPLCA: one process per year, or a non-constant alpha? Only the 'replicated 50 times' baseline is described.
4) What are the r and T values of the aggregator processes ('Entire lifecycle', families)? Is the printed delta = -Y + r a typo for -(Y + r)? The thesis worked example supports -(Y + r).
5) Does any later DyPLCA version support time-varying A and B (e.g. vintage-specific background inventories) natively, rather than through period-specific duplicate processes? I found no evidence that it does.
6) How should renewal counts reconcile with EN 15978? DyPLCA's floor-based batch count sigma would drop a renewal when span/tau is not an integer (my derivation), so explicit event processes appear necessary.
7) Negishi et al. (2019) SI tables SI4, SI10 and SI11, which give the full temporal parameter set and assumptions, were not read.
8) What is the intended form of the discount factor printed as '1/(1+year)x' in Pigné et al. (2020)?
9) Is the DyPLCA tool or its temporal database (IP-protected) still available? Both URLs failed on 2026-11-14.

results.topic: Cardellini, Mutel, Vial and Muys (2018), "Temporalis, a generic method and tool for dynamic Life Cycle Assessment" (Sci. Total Environ. 645:585-595). Covers temporal distributions (TDs) attached to exchanges, relative vs absolute TDs, best-first graph traversal, convolution of TDs along supply-chain paths, the emission timeline, and dynamic characterization (Levasseur et al. 2010 dynamic GWP; Kendall 2012 TAWP). Each item is mapped to process time functions e_i(t), local times tau_i = t - t_i0, convolution, time-dependent matrices and a cumulative C(T).

sources.citation: Cardellini G., Mutel C.L., Vial E., Muys B. (2018). Temporalis, a generic method and tool for dynamic Life Cycle Assessment. Science of the Total Environment 645: 585-595. PMID 30029133.
sources.assumptions: From the abstract (Europe PMC / Semantic Scholar record): the method brings temporal information into both the LCI and the LCIA phases. It uses graph traversal and convolution to compute a temporally differentiated inventory, and it supports several types of dynamic impact assessment. Author keywords: Open Source, Dynamic Modelling, Temporal Differentiation, LCA, Biogenic Carbon, Glulam, Temporal Graph Traversal. The paper's own statements of linearity, time invariance and cut-off could not be checked in its text. Those assumptions are documented in the software documentation, which is a separate source below.
sources.conditions_and_limits: Abstract only. The case study is a cradle-to-grave dynamic LCA of a glulam product, with a sensitivity test of global-warming results to time-explicit LCI data. The abstract reports a 'considerable difference in outcome between the static and dynamic approaches'. Full-text access attempts all failed. ScienceDirect returned 403. The ULB DI-fusion copy (dipot.ulb.ac.be .../284669/1/Elsevier_268296.pdf) is intranet-only. The PSI DORA submitted version returned 403. The Lirias PDF of Cardellini's 2018 KU Leuven PhD thesis returned 404; a search snippet says the thesis contains this paper as a chapter. The paper's notation, equations and equation numbers, the glulam numbers, and its stated cut-off defaults are therefore UNCONFIRMED. No equation is attributed to the paper here.
sources.relevance: This is the anchor reference. Its confirmed content is the architecture: TDs on exchanges, graph traversal plus convolution giving a timeline of elementary flows, then static or dynamic characterization. For the formal operator definitions, use the authors' own code and documentation (next sources) and cite them as software documentation, not as the paper.
sources.time_variables: Unconfirmed in the paper text. The abstract mentions only 'temporal information' and a 'temporally differentiated inventory'.

sources.citation: Cardellini G., Mutel C. (2018). Temporalis: an open source software for dynamic LCA. Journal of Open Source Software 3(24): 612.
sources.assumptions: Full text (2 pages). Temporalis is built on Brightway2. It 'makes use of graph traversal and convolution to solve the inventory'. It can 'resolve time-explicit Life Cycle Inventory (LCI), handle both absolute and relative temporal distributions, as well as exchanges with databases that have no temporal information'. It supports static and dynamic characterization, 'including both distribution over time and characterization as a function of time', for 'any time horizon'. It accounts for biogenic carbon without assuming carbon neutrality and includes forest regrowth.
sources.conditions_and_limits: A software paper with no equations. It cites Levasseur et al. 2010, Kendall 2012, ESPA (Beloin-Saint-Pierre et al. 2014), Collinge et al. 2013 and Tiruta-Barna et al. 2016 as the methodological background.
sources.relevance: Confirms, in full text, the two kinds of time function: relative TDs (local time of the consumer) and absolute TDs (calendar time). It also confirms two dynamic-CF types: a CF that depends on emission date, and a CF that spreads impact over later time, which is a kernel.
sources.time_variables: Relative and absolute temporal distributions; time horizon.

sources.citation: Cardellini G., Mutel C. (2018). Temporalis / bw2temporalis v1.0.1 (2018-04-17): source code and documentation (docs: strategy.rst, traversal.rst, formats.rst, issues.rst, gotcha.rst, index.rst; modules temporal_distribution.py, dynamic_lca.py, timeline.py, dynamic_ia_methods.py, utils.py, dyn_methods/metrics.py, dyn_methods/method_creation.py, dyn_methods/timedependent_lca.py). Archived repository brightway-lca/temporalis (originally bitbucket cardosan/brightway2-temporalis); docs at temporalis.readthedocs.io.

equations.expression: TD = \{(t_k, v_k)\}_{k=1..n},\quad t_k \in timedelta64[s]\ (relative)\ or\ datetime64[s]\ (absolute),\quad v_k \in R
equations.symbols: t_k: time stamp, either an offset relative to the consuming/emitting process (timedelta) or a calendar date (datetime), stored at 1-second resolution; v_k: amount at t_k.
equations.meaning: Definition of a temporal distribution as a discrete set of (time, amount) pairs (class TemporalDistribution(times, values)). Transcribed from code, not from the paper.

equations.expression: \sum_k v_k = amount_{exchange}\ (checked\ with\ rtol = 10^{-4});\quad TD_{default} = \{(0, amount)\};\quad TD \leftarrow -TD\ for\ production/substitution\ exchanges
equations.symbols: amount_exchange: the exchange's scalar amount.
equations.meaning: Normalization rule. In this legacy version a TD carries the exchange's absolute amounts. Docs: 'The sum of all amounts in the temporal distribution should equal the total exchange amount. This is checked automatically.' An exchange with no TD is a single pulse at offset 0.

equations.expression: X \otimes Y = consolidate\{(x_j + y_k,\ u_j w_k)\}_{j,k},\quad i.e.\ (X\otimes Y)(t) = \sum_{j,k:\ x_j + y_k = t} u_j w_k
equations.symbols: X = {(x_j,u_j)}, Y = {(y_k,w_k)}: relative TDs (both timedelta). consolidate: sums amounts that share the same time stamp.
equations.meaning: TemporalDistribution.__mul__ for two relative TDs: discrete convolution by outer sum of times and outer product of amounts. Only allowed for two timedelta TDs.

equations.expression: N_{new} = (N \otimes E)/s\quad (E\ relative);\qquad N_{new} = \{(T_k - t_0,\ e_k \cdot \sum_a n_a / s)\}\quad (E = \{(T_k,e_k)\}\ absolute)
equations.symbols: N = {(tau_a, n_a)}: TD of the consuming node, relative to t0. E: TD of the technosphere exchange. s: production amount of the consumer's reference product (diagonal of the technosphere matrix; normally 1). t0: datetime of the functional unit (default now).
equations.meaning: Propagation rule along an edge (DynamicLCA._calculate_new_td). A relative exchange is convolved with the consumer's TD. An absolute exchange keeps its own calendar dates and only the consumer's total is passed on, so the upstream temporal shape is discarded at that edge.

equations.expression: timeline_b = t_0 + (N \otimes B_b)/s\ (relative\ B_b);\quad (B_b \cdot \sum_a n_a)/s\ (absolute\ B_b);\quad static\ node:\ t_0 + (N \cdot g_b)/s,\ g = rowsum(inventory\ of\ redo\_lci(\{node:1\}))
equations.symbols: B_b: TD of biosphere exchange b of the node. g_b: aggregated (cradle-to-gate) inventory of flow b for one unit of a node in a database flagged static.
equations.meaning: How elementary flows enter the timeline (_add_biosphere_flows, _calculate_bio_td_datetime). Nodes from static databases, and loops past the loop limit, are solved with the matrix LCI, and their whole aggregated inventory is placed at the time stamps of N.

equations.expression: discard\ edge\ if\ |h_{wc}(node, \textstyle\sum N_{new})| < cutoff \cdot |h_{wc}(FU)|;\quad heap\ priority = 1/|h_{wc}(node, \textstyle\sum N_{new})|
equations.symbols: h_wc: static LCIA score computed with the worst-case CF method (redo_lcia). cutoff: default 0.001 in the code signature (docs: '0.1% of the total possible impact'; one docstring says 0.005, which is inconsistent). max_calc_number default 1e4. loop_cutoff default 10.
equations.meaning: Best-first traversal and cut-off (_discard_node, heap ordering): the largest potential contributors are expanded first. An edge is also treated as static when loops[edge] >= loop_cutoff, or when loops[edge] >= 1 and its total amount is >= 1. From reading the code, a discarded edge is simply not pushed to the heap, so its upstream emissions are dropped, not aggregated.

equations.expression: CF_{wc}(b) = |\max_{t \in [lower, upper],\ weekly} \textstyle\sum_m c_{b,m}(t)|\ (dynamic=True);\quad |\sum_m c_{b,m}(lower)|\ (dynamic=False);\ default\ [now, now+100\,yr]
equations.symbols: c_{b,m}(t): the m-th element of the dynamic CF function for flow b evaluated at emission date t.
equations.meaning: Worst-case static method used only to drive the cut-off (DynamicIAMethod.to_worst_case_method, utils.get_maximum_value). Docs: 'if an input is not important ... applying even the highest possible characterization factors, then we can safely exclude it.'

equations.expression: I(t) = \sum_b \sum_n g_b(t_n)\, c_b(t - t_n;\ t_n)\quad (extended\ dynamic\ CF\ returning\ \{(t_n+\Delta_m, c_m)\});\qquad I_{cum}(t) = \sum_{t' \le t} I(t')
equations.symbols: g_b(t_n): timeline amount of flow b at date t_n, summed by (date, flow). c_b: dynamic CF function of the emission datetime, returning either a number or a list of (date, amount) tuples.
equations.meaning: Timeline.characterize_dynamic: each emission is multiplied by a CF that may depend on its date and may be spread over later dates (a kernel). This is a discrete convolution of the emission timeline with an impulse response. Results are summed per date and optionally accumulated (cumulative=True). characterize_static uses a constant CF.

equations.symbols: E_gas: emission TD. RE: radiative efficiency per kg (CO2 1.7517e-15; CH4 1.277e-13*1.65; N2O 3.845e-13; SF6 2.01e-11 W m^-2 kg^-1). D: atmospheric decay as a TD on yearly steps up to the cutoff (1000 yr for the stored constants). tau_x: CH4 12.4, N2O 121, SF6 3200 yr. R_T: AR5 temperature impulse response (ar5_boucher; Olivie and Peters variants op_base/op_low/op_high also present).
equations.meaning: Built-in climate kernels (dyn_methods/metrics.py). Radiative forcing and AGTP are built by TD convolution. Fossil CH4 adds the CO2 from oxidation, (E⊗(0.51/12.4)e^{-t/12.4})·RE_CO2⊗D_CO2. Biogenic CO2 (after Cherubini 2011) uses (p_emis ⊗ IRF) - (NEP ⊗ IRF). Parameters are transcribed from code comments citing IPCC AR5-SM.

equations.expression: GWP_{dyn} = \frac{\int RF_{FU}(t)\,dt\ (trapz,\ from\ first\ result\ year\ to\ year(t_0)+TH)}{\int RF_{CO2}(t)\,dt\ (trapz,\ same\ number\ of\ yearly\ points)}
equations.symbols: RF_FU: non-cumulative yearly radiative-forcing timeline of the FU. RF_CO2: RF of a 1 kg CO2 pulse. TH: time horizon (default 100). t0: year 0.
equations.meaning: dyn_methods.timedependent_lca.time_dependent_LCA, which the docstring says follows Levasseur (2010). Docstring: TH is counted from t0, so emissions before t0 are characterized only up to t0+TH.

sources.assumptions: Docs (index.rst), full text. Abilities: 'Exchanges (technosphere inputs, and biosphere outputs) can be offset in time'; 'Individual exchanges can be split into multiple time steps'; 'Inventory datasets can be given either relative or absolute dates and times'; 'Characterization factors can vary as a function of time'; 'Characterization factors can spread impact over time'. Limitations: 'Inventory datasets cannot change their inputs as a function of time (i.e. are time invariant). This limitation is necessary for the graph traversal to converge' and 'Exchanges must be linear, as in normal matrix-based LCA.' traversal.rst: 'there is no fixed time steps. Each exchange can have an absolute or relative time difference of arbitrary precision'. Absolute dates are useful 'for infrastructure built in the past or data coming from sampling'.
sources.conditions_and_limits: traversal.rst: 'Graph traversal, like power series expansion, can only approximate the solution to a set of linear equations. An infinite number of graph traversal steps would be required to get the precise solution.' Loops (cycles) are traversed until the node impact falls below the cutoff or the loop repeats loop_cutoff times (default 10). Known issue: an activity must produce itself (its reference product). Databases without temporal information should be flagged static; they are then solved by matrix inversion and carry no internal timing. TDs cannot be exported with BW2Package. The timeline is a list of (dt, flow, dataset, amount). Results are reported in fractional years.
sources.relevance: This is the operational definition behind the paper. A TD is a finite Dirac comb e(tau) = sum_k v_k delta(tau - tau_k) in the consumer's local time tau = t - t_consumer for relative TDs, or in calendar time for absolute TDs. Edge propagation is convolution divided by s. The traversal gives the truncated power series of the convolution-algebra inventory. Time invariance of datasets is what makes convolution valid. Time-dependent matrices A(t) are outside Temporalis's scope.
sources.time_variables: t0 (FU datetime, default now); relative offsets (timedelta64, seconds resolution, may be negative, meaning before the consumer); absolute dates (datetime64); emission date t_n; yearly kernel steps; time horizon TH.

sources.citation: Cardellini G. (2018). dLCA: notebooks for 'Temporalis, a generic method and tool for dynamic Life Cycle Assessment' (Artificial Example.ipynb, create_db_glulam.ipynb, calculations_glulam.ipynb; system graph glulam_system5.pdf). GitHub repository cardosan/dLCA.

equations.expression: TD_{forestry\ inputs} = \{(\tau, a/10)\}_{\tau = -90,-80,...,0\ yr};\quad TD_{sawnwood \to glulam} = \{(-2\,yr,\ a)\};\quad TD_{FU \to EoL} = \{(y, \gamma_y)\}_{y=0,1,...}\ (chi^2\ with\ a = k/2,\ b = 2,\ k = 50\,yr)
equations.symbols: a: exchange amount. tau: offset relative to the consuming process. gamma_y: discretized lifetime-decay distribution with mean lifetime k = 50 yr (Marland; Cherubini gamma parametrization, per notebook text).
equations.meaning: Relative TDs used in the glulam case, as built in the notebook (not read in the paper). The forestry technosphere exchanges are spread over a 100-yr rotation, sawnwood is produced 2 years before glulam, and end-of-life is spread by a lifetime distribution.

equations.expression: GWP(t) \approx CRF_{FU}(t)\ /\ cumsum(RF_{CO2,1kg})(t)
equations.symbols: CRF_FU(t): cumulative radiative forcing of the FU (characterize_dynamic with cumulative=True). RF_CO2,1kg: RF of a 1 kg CO2 pulse (co2_rf_td).
equations.meaning: The notebook divides yearly cumulative RF by the cumulated CO2 pulse RF to get a time-dependent GWP-like curve up to 2017+500. The exact alignment of the CO2 reference pulse to t0 is UNCONFIRMED.

sources.assumptions: t0 = 2017-01-01; cutoff = 1e-8; loop_cutoff = 10; worst-case RF method drives the traversal. Biogenic carbon uses rotation 130 yr, chi^2 oxidation profile, emission year 50 (bio_st_decay='chi2', bio_st_emis_yr=50, rot_stand=130). Ecoinvent 3.2 cutoff processes copied into a dynamic 'tempo' database; others flagged static. In the artificial example the dynamic timeline characterized with static CFs is checked against the static LCA score; inputs are given as relative TDs such as [(-3,.2),(-1,.2)] for amount 0.4.
sources.conditions_and_limits: I read the notebook code and markdown, not the stored numerical outputs. These are the authors' analysis notebooks, but the equivalence of their settings with the published paper is UNCONFIRMED.
sources.relevance: A worked example of building-like timing. A product's end-of-life is modelled as a lifetime distribution over years after use, which is the analogue of renewal events and the EoL residual in C(T). The static-versus-timeline check, sum_t g(t) = B A^{-1} f, is a consistency test usable for the C(T) extension.
sources.time_variables: t0 (2017-01-01); yearly offsets; rotation length; mean lifetime k; horizon 500 yr.

sources.citation: Mutel C., Cardellini G. et al. (2023-2026). bw_temporalis: Temporalis library for the Brightway 2.5 LCA framework (temporal_distribution.py, convolution.py, lca.py, lcia/climate.py, README). GitHub brightway-lca/bw_temporalis.

equations.expression: convolve(X,Y):\ date = x_j + y_k,\ amount = u_j w_k,\ consolidated;\quad datetime \otimes timedelta \to datetime;\ timedelta \otimes timedelta \to timedelta
equations.symbols: X, Y: TDs with date arrays (datetime64[s] or timedelta64[s]) and amount arrays.
equations.meaning: The same convolution rule as the legacy code, with typed absolute/relative behaviour (convolution.py).

equations.expression: value_{edge} = TD_{frac} \cdot A[k,p] \cdot sign / s_p;\quad td_{producer} = td_{consumer} \otimes value_{edge};\quad \sum TD_{frac} = 1
equations.symbols: TD_frac: TD whose amounts are fractions of the exchange. A[k,p]: technosphere matrix entry (net amount). sign: -1 for technosphere inputs. s_p: reference product production amount.
equations.meaning: TemporalisLCA.build_timeline: 'Temporal distributions are not density functions - their values are fractions of the exchange amount, and should sum to one.' This normalization differs from the legacy package, where a TD sums to the exchange amount.

equations.expression: FixedTD \otimes relative = convolution;\quad FixedTD \otimes absolute = FixedTD \cdot \sum amount(absolute);\quad absolute \otimes absolute \to second\ operand
equations.symbols: FixedTD: 'An absolute TemporalDistribution that ignores other temporal information.' FixedTimeOfYearTD: a relative TD within one year, pinned to a calendar season of the first available year.
equations.meaning: Explicit semantics of absolute TDs. Calendar dates are fixed, and only the amount of the upstream TD is passed on.

sources.assumptions: Defaults: cutoff 5e-4, biosphere_cutoff 1e-6, max_calc 2000. Traversal uses bw_graph_tools.NewNodeEachVisitGraphTraversal. Databases flagged static and listed static_activity_indices are not traversed. README: the library uses the net amount in the matrices ('caution should be taken in cases where multiple edges with temporal dynamics, especially with different numerical signs, link the same nodes'). Resolution is not finer than seconds.
sources.conditions_and_limits: TDs with more than 1000 points are simplified by k-means clustering (TemporalDistribution.simplify), so long or fine combs are approximated. The built-in CO2 and CH4 CRF functions use a fixed period (default 100 yr) and AR5-type parameters (CO2 RE 1.76e-15, alpha/tau 0.2173/0.2240,394.4/0.2824,36.54/0.2763,4.304).
sources.relevance: A modern reference implementation for the e_i(t) and convolution layer. The fraction-normalized TD corresponds to a probability-like e_i(tau) times the amount. FixedTD corresponds to an event at a fixed calendar time t_i0.
sources.time_variables: starting_datetime (FU), timedelta64[s] / datetime64[s] dates.

sources.citation: Levasseur A., Lesage P., Margni M., Deschenes L., Samson R. (2010). Considering time in LCA: dynamic LCA and its application to global warming impact assessments. Environmental Science & Technology 44(8): 3169-3174. PMID 20302334. Read via its reproduction as Annexe 1 of Levasseur A. (2011), PhD thesis, Ecole Polytechnique de Montreal (PolyPublie 706), which also restates the method in Ch. 2 (Eqs 2.1-2.4, 2.14).

equations.expression: GWP_i^{TH} = \frac{\int_0^{TH} a_i [C_i(t)]\,dt}{\int_0^{TH} a_r [C_r(t)]\,dt}
equations.symbols: TH: time horizon. a: instantaneous radiative forcing per unit mass increase in the atmosphere. C(t): time-dependent atmospheric load of the released gas. i: released gas. r: reference gas CO2. Numerator and denominator are AGWPs.
equations.meaning: Eq. (1), the static GWP.

equations.symbols: Bern carbon-cycle model with 378 ppm background (AR4 / Forster et al. 2007). tau: adjusted lifetime of a non-CO2 gas.
equations.meaning: Eqs (3)-(4), atmospheric load after a pulse.

equations.expression: DCF_i(t)_{cumulative} = AGWP_i(t) = \int_0^{t} a_i [C_i(t)]\,dt;\qquad DCF_i(t)_{instantaneous} = \int_{t-1}^{t} a_i [C_i(t)]\,dt
equations.symbols: DCF_i: dynamic characterization factor of GHG i (W m^-2 kg^-1). One-year time steps.
equations.meaning: Eqs (2) and (5): cumulative and yearly instantaneous dynamic CFs.

equations.expression: GWI(t) = \sum_i GWI_i(t) = \sum_i \sum_{j=0}^{t} [g_i]_j \cdot [DCF_i]_{t-j}
equations.symbols: g_i: dynamic inventory of GHG i (emissions summed per one-year step j). DCF_i: instantaneous DCF. t: time since the beginning of the life cycle.
equations.meaning: Eq. (6): instantaneous radiative-forcing impact as a discrete convolution of the yearly inventory with the DCF kernel. Thesis Eq. 2.3 is identical, GWI_inst(t) = sum_i sum_{j=0}^t g_ij DCF_i(t-j). The inventory is the matrix G (Eq. 2.1, rows = GHG, columns = year), and t = 0 is set at the first emission of the life cycle.

equations.expression: GWI_{cum}(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{t} GWI_{inst}(k);\qquad GWI_{eq} = \frac{GWI_{cum}(TH)}{AGWP_{CO2}(TH)}
equations.symbols: GWI_cum: cumulative radiative forcing (W m^-2 yr). AGWP_CO2(TH): cumulative RF of a 1 kg CO2 pulse at year zero.
equations.meaning: Thesis Eqs 2.4 and 2.14. Cumulative impact, and conversion to kg CO2-eq for comparison with static GWP.

equations.expression: NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{TH} \frac{GHG_t}{(1+r)^t};\qquad \%IC_{ethanol} = \frac{NPV_{ethanol} - NPV_{gasoline}}{NPV_{gasoline}} \times 100
equations.symbols: GHG_t: total GHG (here RF) for year t. r: discount rate (0 allowed). TH: time horizon.
equations.meaning: Eqs (7)-(8) of the biofuel case: optional discounting and percentage impact change.

sources.assumptions: Same atmospheric models as the IPCC GWPs (AR4). One-year discretization. Linear superposition of pulse responses. A fixed time horizon fixes the integration boundary in calendar time rather than per emission, which corrects the time-frame inconsistency illustrated with a 75-year-lifetime building (Fig. 2).
sources.conditions_and_limits: Read as the manuscript reproduced in the author's thesis, not the ACS typeset version, which returned 403. Equation numbering and constants in the published version are therefore UNCONFIRMED, although the Annexe is presented as the article. Developed for global warming only. Discounting is treated as a policy choice outside the method.
sources.relevance: Gives the dynamic-LCIA layer as an explicit discrete convolution: impact(t) = sum_j g(j) K(t-j). For the building model, the C(T) year cells, renewal events and EoL residual form g_i(j), and GWI_cum(T) is the dynamic counterpart of the cumulative C(T). The 75-year building example is directly analogous.
sources.time_variables: t (years since the first emission); j (emission year index); TH (time horizon); r (discount rate).

sources.citation: Kendall A. (2012). Time-adjusted global warming potentials for LCA and carbon footprints. International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment 17(8): 1042-1049.

equations.expression: GWP_{AT} = \frac{\int_0^{AT} RF_i\,dt}{\int_0^{AT} RF_{CO2}\,dt} = \frac{CRF_i}{CRF_{CO2}}
equations.symbols: AT: analytical time horizon. RF: radiative forcing, a function of the gas's atmospheric decay and radiative efficiency. i: GHG converted to CO2e. CRF: cumulative radiative forcing.
equations.meaning: Eq. (1), the conventional GWP.

equations.expression: TAWP_{AT}(y) = \frac{\int_0^{AT-y} RF_i(t)\,dt}{\int_0^{AT} RF_{CO2}(t)\,dt}
equations.symbols: y: year in which the emission occurs (reference time year 0 = today). AT - y: years the emission remains in the atmosphere by the end of AT.
equations.meaning: Eq. (2). Only the numerator's integration boundary is shortened for emission timing; the denominator stays the CO2 pulse at year 0. Result in CO2e 'today'.

equations.expression: CO_2e = mass\ of\ emission_i \times TAWP_{AT}(y)
equations.symbols: mass of emission_i: mass of GHG i emitted in year y.
equations.meaning: Eq. (3). For a life cycle, CO2e is the sum over all (i, y) of mass times TAWP.

sources.assumptions: CRF model built from IPCC AR4 lifetimes, radiative efficiencies and methane indirect effects. CO2 is the reference gas and year 0 the reference time. Small mismatches with IPCC GWPs come from the limited significant digits reported by IPCC (e.g. TAWP500(y=0) for CH4 deviates by 0.08 kg CO2e).
sources.conditions_and_limits: TAWPs cannot be reduced to a single scaling factor, because y is a second variable. An Excel tool (TAWPv1.0) and best-fit polynomials for AT = 20/30/50/100/500 are given in the ESM, which I did not read. The method favours pushing emissions later. Building case: production and construction 4,360.5 t CO2e at year 0, use phase 1,737.5 t/yr for 75 yr, decommissioning 324 t, all treated as CO2. TAWP100 gives 93,315 t CO2e and TAWP500 gives 127,591 t CO2e, against 135,000 t by simple summation. PAS2050 general case gives 83,884.
sources.relevance: A closed-form dynamic characterization that can be applied directly to a C(T) built from constants, year cells, renewal events and EoL. Each term at time y is weighted by TAWP_AT(y). For a single pulse at y, TAWP_AT(y) equals Levasseur's GWI_cum(AT)/AGWP_CO2(AT) with t = 0 at the reference year (my own derivation, not stated in either paper).
sources.time_variables: y (emission year), AT (analytical time horizon), reference year 0.

sources.citation: Muller A., Diepers T., Jakobs A., Cardellini G., von der Assen N., Guinee J., Steubing B. (2025). Time-explicit life cycle assessment: a flexible framework for coherent consideration of temporal dynamics. International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment 30(12): 3052-3071 (volume/pages from PMC XML metadata).

equations.expression: h = C B A^{-1} f
equations.symbols: f: demand vector; A: technology matrix (a_kp); B: biosphere matrix (b_jp); C: characterization matrix; h: impacts.
equations.meaning: Eq. (1), static LCA.

equations.expression: h = \sum_{t_0}^{t_e} C_t B_t A_t^{-1} f_t
equations.symbols: t: distinct time point at which the system state is known; t0, te: start and end of the analysis.
equations.meaning: Eq. (3), Collinge et al. (2013): one matrix set per timestep. It ignores supply-chain lags between timesteps.

equations.symbols: * : matrices expanded with 'products @ timesteps' and 'processes @ timesteps' row-column pairs (temporalized processes, temporal markets).
equations.meaning: Eq. (4), time-explicit LCA. The timeline of intermediate flows from rTD convolution is used to extend the matrices, so time-dependent process data can be linked.

sources.assumptions: Secondary description of Temporalis, read in full text: 'we use rTDs as implemented in Cardellini et al. (2018). A rTD reflects how the total amount of a flow is distributed across time'. For intermediate flows, rTDs give when product k is demanded relative to its consuming process p, and for elementary flows when b is emitted relative to p. 'As time in LCA is inherently discrete ... continuous inputs or emissions can be discretized by sampling the supply or emission functions.' The rTDs are 'convolved along the supply chain', starting from the FU at an absolute time. 'Unlike Cardellini et al. (2018), we construct an absolute timeline of intermediate flows, rather than that of elementary flows.' The best-first traversal was moved to bw_graph_tools. Temporal markets interpolate linearly by default between time-specific background databases.
sources.conditions_and_limits: bw_timex stops temporal convolution at the background database. With evolving supply chains, best-first cut-off may exclude important branches, so a 'sufficiently low cutoff threshold should be selected'. Large data requirements. Supports only outflow-driven models.
sources.relevance: Supplies the time-dependent matrix layer (A*(t), B*(t)) that Temporalis lacks because of its time-invariance assumption. This is the route for the 'time-dependent matrices' part of the chapter. It also notes that lifetime distributions can be modelled as rTDs.
sources.time_variables: Absolute time of the FU; timesteps of temporalized processes; time-specific database years.

sources.citation: Beloin-Saint-Pierre D., Heijungs R., Blanc I. (2014). The ESPA (Enhanced Structural Path Analysis) method: a solution to an implementation challenge for dynamic life cycle assessment studies. International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment 19(4): 861-871 (bibliographic data as cited in the JOSS paper).
sources.assumptions: Secondary sources (Temporalis docs strategy.rst; Muller et al. 2025): ESPA 'uses power series expansion and convolution to propagate relative temporal differences through the supply chain'. In graph terms it is a breadth-first search, while Temporalis uses best-first. It introduced 'process-relative temporal distributions'.
sources.conditions_and_limits: The full text was not read: HAL served a bot-challenge page. Its equations are UNCONFIRMED and none are given here.
sources.relevance: Methodological origin of 'convolution of relative TDs plus series expansion of (I - A)^{-1}'. It is the formal counterpart of Temporalis's traversal and the natural source for a matrix-of-TDs formulation.
sources.time_variables: Process-relative temporal distributions (per secondary sources).

results.synthesis:
Read levels: [FT] = full text, [ABS] = abstract only, [SEC] = secondary source, [CODE] = authors' source code or documentation read in full. [DER] = my own derivation, not stated in any source.

1. What the Temporalis paper itself confirms [ABS]. It adds temporal information to both LCI and LCIA. It computes a temporally differentiated inventory by graph traversal and convolution and supports several dynamic LCIA types. The case study is a cradle-to-grave glulam product, and static and dynamic results differ considerably. The full text could not be accessed, so the paper's own equations, notation and glulam numbers are UNCONFIRMED. The JOSS paper [FT] confirms the same features: relative and absolute TDs, databases without temporal information, CFs that depend on time or spread impact over time, any time horizon, and biogenic carbon without assumed neutrality.

2. Temporal distribution as a function e(t) [CODE]. A TD is a finite set of (time, amount) pairs {(t_k, v_k)}. Read as a function, it is a Dirac comb e(tau) = sum_k v_k delta(tau - tau_k) [DER].
- A relative TD uses timedelta stamps. These are offsets in the local time of the consuming or emitting process, tau = t - t_consumer, at 1-second resolution, and negative means earlier.
- An absolute TD uses datetime stamps, i.e. calendar time t.
- Normalization differs between versions. In legacy bw2temporalis, sum_k v_k equals the exchange amount (checked to rtol 1e-4), and the default is {(0, amount)}. In bw_temporalis the amounts are fractions summing to 1, multiplied by the matrix amount, and 'not density functions'.
- So e_i(tau) = amount_i * phi_i(tau), where phi_i is a discrete probability-like mass function. A continuous profile is represented by sampling it (stated in Muller et al. 2025 [FT]).

3. Convolution rule [CODE]. (X ⊗ Y)(t) = sum over j,k with x_j + y_k = t of u_j * w_k, with equal time stamps consolidated.
- Relative edge: N_new = (N ⊗ E)/s, where N is the consumer's TD relative to t0 and s is its reference-product amount.
- Path: the TD at node n is t0 + δ ⊗ E_{FU,1} ⊗ E_{1,2} ⊗ ... ⊗ E_{n-1,n} / prod(s).
- Elementary flow b: g_b(t) = t0 + sum over paths of (N_path ⊗ B_{n,b})/s_n.
- The traversal therefore evaluates the series g = B ⊛ sum_k Ã^{⊛k} ⊛ f δ_{t0} in a convolution algebra, where Ã is the matrix of normalized TDs, truncated by the cut-off [DER]. The docs confirm that traversal 'like power series expansion, can only approximate the solution to a set of linear equations'.
- If all TDs equal δ_0, this reduces to static g = B A^{-1} f. The authors' artificial-example notebook checks exactly this: the timeline characterized with static CFs against the static score.

4. How absolute TDs fix calendar dates [CODE]. If E is absolute, N_new = E * (sum of N)/s, with times T_k - t0. The consumer's temporal shape collapses to its total, and the exchange happens at the given dates whenever the consumer happens. bw_temporalis makes this explicit with FixedTD, an absolute TD that 'ignores other temporal information', and FixedTimeOfYearTD (seasonal pinning). Use cases named in the docs: past infrastructure, sampled data.

5. Assumptions [CODE docs, FT].
- Linearity: 'Exchanges must be linear, as in normal matrix-based LCA'.
- Time invariance: 'Inventory datasets cannot change their inputs as a function of time ... necessary for the graph traversal to converge'. This is also what makes the convolution valid, because the same relative TD applies wherever a process sits in time [DER].
- Net matrix amounts (bw_temporalis).
- Each activity must produce its own reference product.
- Static databases (e.g. ecoinvent) are solved by matrix inversion. Their aggregated inventory is placed at the consumer's time stamps, with no internal timing.

6. Cut-off of traversal [CODE].
- Best-first: a heap ordered by 1/|score|.
- An edge is discarded if |h_wc(node, amount)| < cutoff * |h_wc(FU)|. The legacy defaults are cutoff = 0.001 (one docstring says 0.005), max_calc 10,000 and loop_cutoff 10. bw_temporalis uses cutoff 5e-4, biosphere_cutoff 1e-6 and max_calc 2000.
- With dynamic CFs, h_wc uses worst-case static CFs, the maximum of the CF function over [now, now+100 yr], to bound the score.
- In the legacy code a discarded branch is simply not expanded, so its emissions are dropped. The truncation error therefore makes C(T) an underestimate by roughly cutoff-sized pieces; the docs do not quantify this.
- bw_temporalis also clusters TDs with more than 1000 points (k-means), which approximates long or fine time combs.

7. Timeline and dynamic characterization.
- The timeline [CODE] is a list of (date, flow, dataset, amount). Static characterization multiplies by constant CFs. Dynamic characterization applies CF functions of the emission date, which may return a spread kernel {(t_n + Δ_m, c_m)}, so I(t) = sum_b sum_n g_b(t_n) c_b(t - t_n).
- The built-in RF and AGTP kernels are TD convolutions [CODE]: RF = (E * RE) ⊗ D, and AGTP = RF ⊗ R_T.
- Levasseur et al. 2010 [FT]: DCF_i(t) = ∫_{t-1}^{t} a_i C_i dt; GWI(t) = sum_i sum_{j=0}^{t} g_i(j) DCF_i(t-j); GWI_cum(t) = sum_{k≤t} GWI_inst(k); GWI_eq = GWI_cum(TH)/AGWP_CO2(TH). This is a discrete convolution of the yearly inventory with an impulse response, with t = 0 at the first emission.
- Kendall 2012 [FT]: TAWP_AT(y) = ∫_0^{AT-y} RF_i / ∫_0^{AT} RF_CO2, and CO2e = sum of mass times TAWP_AT(y). For a pulse at y this equals Levasseur's GWI_cum(AT)/AGWP_CO2(AT) [DER].
- Kendall's commercial building: 4,360.5 t at year 0, 1,737.5 t/yr for 75 yr, 324 t at decommissioning. TAWP100 gives 93,315 t CO2e against 135,000 t by simple summation, about 30 % lower; TAWP500 gives 127,591 t.

8. Mapping to the building C(T) model [DER]. Write each component as e_i(tau_i) with tau_i = t - t_i0:
- constants: v δ(tau);
- year cells: sum_{y=1}^{T} q_y δ(tau - y);
- renewal events at k*L_i: sum_k m_i δ(tau - k L_i), or a lifetime distribution as in the authors' glulam EoL (a chi-square with mean 50 yr);
- EoL residual: r δ(tau - T).
Upstream supply chains enter by convolution with their relative TDs. Then:
- static-CF cumulative: C(T) = sum_b c_b ∫_{t0}^{t0+T} g_b(t) dt, which is Temporalis's cumulative characterize_static evaluated at T;
- dynamic: C_dyn(T) = GWI_cum(T)/AGWP_CO2(TH), or the TAWP-weighted sum.
Temporalis cannot represent time-dependent matrices A(t), B(t), for example decarbonizing electricity for year cells or future replacement products. That needs the matrix expansion h* = C* B* A*^{-1} f* of Muller et al. 2025 [FT], or explicit absolute-dated processes.
results.open_questions:
1. The full text of Cardellini et al. (2018) was not accessed. The publisher page, the ULB copy (intranet only) and the PSI DORA copy were all blocked, and the Lirias PDF of the thesis returned 404. Unconfirmed: the paper's own symbols for TDs and convolution, its equation numbering, any matrix formulation, the cut-off value used in the paper, the glulam results and the sensitivity-test design. Whether the paper itself states time invariance and linearity (as opposed to the software docs) is also unconfirmed. Next step: get the publisher PDF or the KU Leuven thesis chapter and replace the code-derived equations with the paper's own.
2. From the code, branches below the cut-off are dropped, not aggregated. Whether the paper quantifies the resulting truncation error, or proposes adding back the residual (for example static LCI of discarded nodes), is unconfirmed.
3. Which dynamic GWP the paper uses is unclear. The notebook divides the cumulative RF curve by a cumulated CO2 pulse, which gives a time-varying denominator. time_dependent_LCA instead uses ∫ RF_FU / ∫ RF_CO2 over TH counted from t0. Which one the paper reports, and how emissions before t0 are handled, is unconfirmed.
4. The legacy cut-off default is inconsistent: 0.001 in the signature and the docs ('0.1%'), 0.005 in one docstring.
5. TD normalization differs between bw2temporalis (sum = exchange amount) and bw_temporalis (sum = 1, fractions). The chapter must pick one convention for e_i(t).
6. Not read: the Levasseur 2010 published ACS version (read via the thesis Annexe), so its equation numbering and constants are unverified against print; Kendall's ESM (TAWPv1.0, polynomials); and the ESPA equations, because HAL served a bot challenge.
