equations.symbols: y: year in the time horizon, counted from the year of construction.
equations.meaning: Inventory dynamics: future (renewal and end-of-life) emissions are scaled down exponentially for technological progress. The authors call these possible development paths, not predictions; the decay factors were varied from 0.5% to 4% in the GSA.

equations.expression: delay weighting for a T-year TH: w_T(y) = 2 - e^{(\ln 2 / T) y};  20-yr: 2 - e^{0.0347 y};  100-yr: 2 - e^{0.00693 y};  500-yr: 2 - e^{0.00139 y}   (Table 1)
equations.symbols: T: time horizon (years). y: year of emission within the TH.
equations.meaning: Characterization dynamics, simplified. The weight falls from 1 at y = 0 to 0 at y = T and approximates the cumulative radiative forcing within the TH relative to an emission at year 0. It was fitted to IRF-based weights computed for every tenth year with the method of Levasseur et al.; for 1 kg CO2e per year over a 100-year TH it is 0.2% off the IRF calculation.

equations.symbols: f_CR: first derivative of the Chapman-Richards growth function. k, p: growth-rate and catabolism parameters. m_{CO2,i}: mass of stored CO2 in inventory product i. y: years in the rotation period (100 years assumed).
equations.meaning: Time profile of biogenic CO2 uptake by forest regrowth after harvest, attributed to the regrowth.

equations.expression: carbonation uptake profile 1 - e^{-0.03 y}, normalized over the years y of the building lifetime; total 0.1 kg CO2 per kg cement over 100 years; cement content 17% of concrete
equations.symbols: y: year of building lifetime.
equations.meaning: Time profile of cement carbonation (B_cem). End-of-life carbonation is not attributed to the building.

equations.expression: subpart emissions (Table 2): A = Q\alpha_{pro}, Q\alpha_{tra}, Q\alpha_{was};  B = Q\beta_{pro}, Q\beta_{tra}, Q\beta_{was}, Q\beta_{bio}, Q\beta_{cem};  C = Q\gamma_{tra}, Q\gamma_{was}, Q\gamma_{bio};  adjusted future (B+C) = Q\beta_{pro}\omega_{pro}\tau_{pro}, Q(\beta_{tra}+\gamma_{tra})\omega_{tra}\tau_{tra}, Q(\beta_{was}+\gamma_{was})\omega_{was}\tau_{was}, Q(\beta_{bio}+\gamma_{bio})\tau_{bio}, Q\beta_{cem}\tau_{cem}
equations.symbols: Q: total mass of the subpart. alpha, beta, gamma: mass-weighted mean emission intensities for the construction (A), operation (B) and end-of-life (C) phases, without dynamic effects. omega: tech factors. tau: delay factors (emission-weighted averages, computed as adjusted / unadjusted subpart results). NOTE: in this paper tau is a delay factor, not a local time.
equations.meaning: Aggregate metrics that let static building LCA results be rescaled for technology and delay effects by multiplication.

sources.assumptions: Replacement years are random variables with variance increasing over time (chi-square distributed). The 'no cut-off' version keeps part of the replacement emissions after the building lifetime because the lifetime is itself uncertain. 50% of stored carbon is oxidized at end of life, and technological progress reduces that fraction by about 1% per year. Process-based attributional LCA; functional unit is 1 m2 of heated floor area over given lifetimes and THs. 20 Norwegian case buildings, harmonized from a 60-year lifetime. Variance-based (Sobol) GSA with SALib. Emission sources: production, transport, waste incineration, biogenic uptake, carbonation; modules A, B and C per EN 15978-like logic.
sources.conditions_and_limits: Inventories use GWP100 CO2e (from EPDs), so the delay method is fully consistent only for the 100-year TH; other THs are consistent for CO2 but not for the non-CO2 share. Indicator: dynamic GWP within a TH only (no temperature or feedbacks). The GSA depends on the inventory and assumed ranges. Results are representative of Norwegian low-emission buildings. Operational energy is excluded. With an infinite TH, future emissions are highly uncertain and should not guide policy.
sources.relevance: Closest to the C(T) structure. Construction is the constant; renewal events at replacement years (stochastic t_i0) are weighted by tech decay (an inventory time function of calendar or building time) and by the delay weight (a characterization function of time-to-horizon); the end-of-life residual gets the same treatment. Cumulative and annual profiles are given for TH = 20, 100, 500 years and infinite. The multiplicative separable form (omega(y) times w_T(y)) is a special case of a convolution with a cumulative IRF, evaluated at T.
sources.time_variables: Year y counted from construction; building lifetime (60, 80, 100 years); material service life l; replacement years (random, chi-square); time horizon T (20/100/500 years, infinite); forest rotation period (100 years); technology half-lives (19-69 years).

sources.citation: Hoxha, E., Passer, A., Saade, M.R.M., Trigaux, D., Shuttleworth, A., Pittau, F., Allacker, K., Habert, G. (2020). Biogenic carbon in buildings: a critical overview of LCA methods. Buildings and Cities, 1(1), 504-524.

equations.symbols: C_CO2(t): decay pattern of a CO2 pulse (e.g. 1 kg). a_0 = 0.217, a_1 = 0.259, a_2 = 0.338, a_3 = 0.186. tau_1 = 172.9 y, tau_2 = 18.5 y, tau_3 = 1.186 y (perturbation times). Bern model, 378 ppm background.
equations.meaning: Impulse response function (IRF) of CO2.
First-order decay IRF for the other GHGs. CO is accounted as CO2.

equations.expression: DCF_{inst,GHG}(t - t_j) = \int_{t_j}^{t} A_{GHG} C_{GHG}(t) dt   (5, as printed)
equations.symbols: A_GHG: specific radiative forcing per unit mass (A_CO2 = 1.76e-15, A_CH4 = 1.28e-13, A_N2O = 3.90e-13 W m^-2 kg^-1). t_j: time of occurrence of the emission. t: time.
equations.meaning: Instantaneous dynamic characterization factor 'formulated by Levasseur et al. (2013)'. The integration bounds are as reconstructed from the PDF text; whether this matches Levasseur's per-time-step integration is unconfirmed here.

equations.expression: GWI_{inst,GHG}(t - t_j) = \sum_{GHG} g_{GHG}(t_j) \cdot DCF_{inst,GHG}(t - t_j)   (6);   GWI_{cum}(t) = \sum_{t_j=0}^{t} GWI_{inst,GHG}(t - t_j)   (7)
equations.symbols: g_GHG(t_j): emission (minus removal) of the GHG at time t_j. t: time horizon at which the cumulative impact is evaluated.
equations.meaning: Discrete convolution of the emission time series with the impulse-response-based characterization, a function of time since emission.

equations.expression: GW_{dynamic}(t) = GWI_{cum}(t) / AGWP_{CO2}(t),  with AGWP_{CO2}(t) = \int A_{CO2} C_{CO2}(t) dt (over [0, t]; bounds partly garbled in the PDF text extraction)   (8)
equations.symbols: AGWP_CO2(t): absolute GWP of a 1 kg CO2 pulse over the same time.
equations.meaning: Expresses the cumulative radiative forcing in CO2-equivalents at the chosen horizon.

sources.assumptions: Compares the 0/0 and -1/+1 static approaches with dynamic Levasseur-type accounting, in two variants: uptake before harvest or by regrowth after harvest. Restricted to CO, CO2, CH4 and N2O. Timber-building case study. Discrete time step t = year of impact occurrence.
sources.conditions_and_limits: LULUC impacts and carbon-storage credits are missing from most methods. The -1/+1 approach with truncated system boundaries can yield net-negative GW. Results deviate by 16% between methods at building scale and by 35-200% at component scale. The authors find the dynamic approach the most robust and transparent and recommend it. Equations (1)-(2) (static GW_0/0, GW_-1/+1) are garbled in text extraction and are not reproduced.
sources.relevance: Gives in explicit discrete form the characterization convolution needed for C(T): C_dyn(T) = sum over emission times t_j <= T of g(t_j) * DCF(T - t_j). Here t_j is the emission time (from renewal events or year cells) and T - t_j is the local impact time. It complements the inventory-side convolution of Pigné et al.
sources.time_variables: Discrete time step t (year of impact occurrence); emission time t_j; time horizon t; GHG perturbation times; rotation period and uptake timing (before or after harvest).

sources.citation: Salati, M., Costa, A.A., Silvestre, J.D. (2025; published online 28 Dec 2024). A Comprehensive Review of Dynamic Life Cycle Assessment for Buildings: Exploring Key Processes and Methodologies. Sustainability, 17(1), 159.
sources.assumptions: Google Scholar, 2019-2024: an initial 100 articles (20 reviews, 80 research), 50 analysed. Scope: technical and environmental dynamic variables affecting building carbon, bottom-up; social and cultural factors and functional-unit dynamics excluded. Eight building-scale dynamic parameters: energy evolution (energy mix, efficiency), temperature change (climate change effects on heating and cooling), technological advances, carbonation (and biogenic carbon), material flows from replacements, waste recycling rates, plus CFs and WFs as coefficients. Eight approaches: material-specific dynamic frameworks; integrated assessment and SD models; dynamic inventory tools (DyPLCA, graph search); spatiotemporal models; emerging materials and prospective LCA; simplified methods (Bath spreadsheet, LCAbyg in Python, FutureBuilt Zero); optimisation and uncertainty (Monte Carlo, MOO); electricity-generation dynamics. Types per da Costa et al.: dynamic system boundary, dynamic inventory, dynamic modelling/characterisation. Post-assessment vs predictive assessment (after Su et al. 2022).
sources.conditions_and_limits: Building assessment periods range from 50 to 100 years. Most studies vary only one or a few variables (often energy mix). Standardization aids adoption but may hinder methodological advances. Cut-off criteria for which dynamics to include are needed, since it is not feasible to include all variables. Operational models that compute inventories with dynamic variables are still early. Weighting factors need further study. Parameter frequencies are biased by the article selection.
sources.relevance: An up-to-date inventory of building dynamic variables, nearly all on the inventory side (energy mix, climate-driven operational demand, technology, replacements, recycling, carbonation). Characterization dynamics appear mostly as dynamic CFs or time-dependent GWP. Useful for deciding which e_i(t) and B(t) entries to make time-dependent in C(T).
sources.time_variables: Assessment period (50-100 years); service life of products (e.g. HVAC 15 years, wood 100 years); replacement intervals (e.g. PV at 5/10/15/20 years); insulation service life 25/50/70/75 years; calendar projections (e.g. 2020-2050, 2060); evaluation point (post vs predictive); seasonal and annual variation; time horizon.

sources.citation: Hosamo, H., Coelho, G.B.A., Buvik, E., Drissi, S., Kraniotis, D. (2024). Building sustainability through a novel exploration of dynamic LCA uncertainty: Overview and state of the art. Building and Environment, 264, 111922.
sources.assumptions: Abstract and relevant sections read; I searched and skimmed the sections on temporal uncertainty and service life, not every section. 430 papers refined to 180. Uncertainty is split into parametric, model, scenario and temporal uncertainty. Temporal uncertainty concerns variation of impacts over a building's lifespan through ageing, maintenance and end of life. Service life is typically modelled with a normal distribution; service-life uncertainty may account for up to 20% of a building's GWP (citing their ref. [147]). Service-life prediction methods: geometric service-life modelling, Markov deterioration curves, statistical analysis. The chosen Reference Study Period (RSP) shifts the relative importance of life-cycle phases. The paper proposes a hybrid process/input-output framework and integration of BIM, IoT and machine learning.
sources.conditions_and_limits: A broad uncertainty review with no formal dynamic-LCA equations. Several statements are qualitative.
sources.relevance: Supports treating renewal times t_i0 and service lives l_i as random variables (cf. Resch's chi-square timing) and the study period/RSP as a variable T in C(T). Mainly inventory-side (service life, maintenance, operational energy, transport) temporal uncertainty.
sources.time_variables: Service life (designed vs actual); Reference Study Period; maintenance and replacement cycles; life-cycle stages A1-D; operational time series.

sources.citation: Slavkovic, K., Stephan, A., Mulders, G.Y. (2022). Dynamic Life Cycle Assessment - Parameters for scenario development in prospective environmental modelling of building stocks. IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science, 1122, 012027.
sources.assumptions: ScienceDirect search: 102 papers, 12 analysed in depth (prospective building-stock DLCA). Eight dynamic parameters, with the number of studies: stock development (new construction, replacement, renovation, retrofit, demolition; 6), energy mix (6), technological development (6), biogenic carbon (5), carbonation (3), occupants (3), population growth (3), degradation of materials and systems (1). Five methods for evolutions (32 applications): hypothesised deterministic (10), hypothesised probabilistic (7), parametric equations (4), interpolation/extrapolation (3), output as a function of input evolutions (1), plus combinations.
sources.conditions_and_limits: Small sample. Energy-mix pathways mostly end in 2050 and follow policy targets, which may not capture shocks. Biogenic-carbon allocation (storage before or after harvest) gives inconsistent results and is often poorly reported. Carbonation in use is minor (<2%; about 20% after crushing). Occupant parameters are limited to residential buildings. Interdependence between parameters needs research.
sources.relevance: Separates the period of analysis (the effective period over which the stock is modelled, typically to 2050) from the time horizon (the period over which impacts are modelled, up to 500 years). This is the same split as study period T vs impact horizon in the C(T) extension. Stock development equals event processes (renovation, replacement) in calendar time.
sources.time_variables: Period of analysis (POA); time horizon (TH, up to 500 years); calendar target years (2050); cohorts and archetypes.

results.synthesis:
1. A common skeleton (my formalization, not an equation from any single paper). Three formal families appear in the sources read in full.
(a) Time-indexed matrices solved independently per calendar time step. Collinge et al. 2013 (equation known only from a secondary source): impacts = sum_{t=t0}^{te} C_t B_t A_t^-1 f_t. Su et al. 2022, Eq. 1 (full text): TEI(T,S) = sum EF_i(T,S) BI_{i-j}(T,S) CF_{j-n}(T,S) NF_n WF_n(T,S), with a dynamic background BI_El-j(T,S) = sum_k P_k(T,S) BI_k-j. This is the year-cell generalization of C(T): C(T) = sum_{t<=T} h(t). It is synchronous: no process lag and no impact lag.
(b) Process-relative time functions combined by convolution along the supply chain. Beloin-Saint-Pierre 2020 describes this for ESPA, DyPLCA and Temporalis; Pigné et al. 2020 ESM gives the equations. Each process has alpha_i(t) and beta_k,i(t) defined from its own zero time t_0,i, normalized so their integrals equal the static a_ii and b_ki (Eqs. 3-4). Upstream profiles are placed at t_0,consumer - r - delta + (x-1)tau, i.e. shifted copies forming a discrete convolution with the delivery schedule (Eqs. 11-12). The result is gamma_k(t) = sum_ij beta_k,ij(t), whose integral recovers the static g_k (Eqs. 13-15). This is exactly e_i(tau_i) with tau_i = t - t_i0, plus convolution between processes.
(c) Characterization by impulse response. Hoxha et al. 2020 (Levasseur-type), Eqs. 5-8: GWI_cum(t) = sum_{t_j<=t} sum_GHG g_GHG(t_j) DCF_GHG(t - t_j) and GW_dynamic = GWI_cum / AGWP_CO2. This is a discrete convolution of the inventory time series with the characterization kernel, written in the local impact time t - t_j. Resch et al. 2021 approximate it with a separable weight w_T(y) = 2 - e^{(ln2/T) y} for an emission in year y within horizon T, fitted to IRF results and valid for CO2-dominant, GWP_T-consistent inventories.
Suggested combined form for the chapter (my formalization): C_dyn(T) = sum_k integral_0^T CF_k^cum(T - t; t) * gamma_k(t) dt, with gamma_k(t) = sum_i s_i(t) beta_k,i(t - t_i0) and time-dependent coefficients a_ij(t), b_ki(t). The static C(T) is recovered when the beta are Dirac pulses at t_i0 (construction, renewal events at n*l_i, end-of-life residual), the coefficients are time-invariant and CF^cum is constant (infinite or ignored horizon). Pigné's integral normalization (Eq. 14) is the consistency test.

2. Time variables found across the sources.
- Calendar time t or T: Collinge; Su 2022 (year T); Beloin's calendar-based periods of validity.
- Building age or time since construction y: Resch.
- Study period, assessment TH or RSP: Lueddeckens' TH of the assessment; Hosamo's RSP; Slavkovic's period of analysis.
- Inventory TH, i.e. the period in which emissions occur: Lueddeckens.
- Impact or characterization TH: Lueddeckens; Beloin (20/100/500/1000 years or infinite); Negishi's 500-year span.
- Service life and renewal: deterministic in most work; random chi-square replacement times with no cut-off in Resch; normal service-life distributions in Hosamo.
- Emission time t_j: Hoxha.
- Process zero time and period of occurrence, production period r, supply delay delta, supply period tau, functioning span, back-time limit: Pigné/DyPLCA; Beloin.
- Temporal resolution: hour to century (Beloin); monthly is sufficient for buildings in two studies.
- Evaluation point, separating post-assessment from predictive assessment: Su 2022; Salati.

3. Classification of dynamic aspects.
INVENTORY DYNAMICS (technosphere, DLCI):
- Foreground use flows f(t): occupancy and occupant behaviour (Su 2017 abstract; Negishi 2018 abstract; Collinge, secondary), household size and usage (Su 2021 EIAR, secondary), climate-change-driven heating and cooling (Salati; Hosamo), degradation of insulation and HVAC (Negishi abstract; Slavkovic; Salati).
- Background B(t): grid or energy-mix decarbonisation, the most studied (Su 2022 Eq. 2; Sohn's DSys; Slavkovic; Salati); technological progress, e.g. Resch's e^{-0.01y}, e^{-0.02y}, e^{-0.037y} (Su 2017; Sohn's DPI); waste treatment and recycling rates (Su 2021 EIAR; Resch); regulations (Negishi; Collinge).
- Timing and structure: renewal and replacement events and service life (Resch; Hosamo); renovation, retrofit and demolition as stock development (Slavkovic); intra-process temporal distributions and supply delays (Pigné/DyPLCA); biogenic uptake timing (Resch's Chapman-Richards; Hoxha); carbonation (Resch); dynamic scope and functional unit (Sohn; Beloin).
CHARACTERIZATION DYNAMICS (ecosphere, DLCIA):
- Time-dependent CFs from IRFs and cumulative radiative forcing, GWP or temperature indicators (Hoxha; Negishi 2019; Fouquet abstract; Resch's delay factor).
- Choice of TH and its consistency with the assessment TH (Lueddeckens' year-99 to 199-year example; Beloin).
- Changing background concentrations, ecosystem sensitivity, exposed population (Lueddeckens citing Collinge; Beloin).
- Toxicity fate dynamics (Beloin citing Shimako).
- Spatial CFs (Su 2022).
VALUATION DYNAMICS, beyond characterization:
- Dynamic weighting: Su 2017/2019; Su 2022 Eqs. 4-6, distance-to-target.
- Dynamic normalization: rare; Su 2022 keeps it static.
- Discounting: Lueddeckens; a finite TH is equivalent to discounting at 0% then 100%.
Caveat: Resch's 'weighting factors' for delay are physically characterization (TH-consistent cumulative radiative forcing), not valuation.

4. Consensus and limits.
- Dynamic inventory and dynamic characterization both improve accuracy (Lueddeckens).
- Most DLCAs are partial: 93% in Sohn, 73% inventory-only. A partial DLCA can bias comparisons.
- Data availability (process-relative distributions are missing from databases) and tool support are the main barriers (Beloin; Sohn; Salati).
- Static CFs are often kept for lack of data (Su 2022).
- Characterization windows must end at the study horizon to avoid inconsistency (Lueddeckens; Resch). Under a fixed-window GWP100 applied to a dynamic inventory, late renewal emissions are over-weighted.
- Prospective scenarios add uncertainty; Fouquet suggests using them as a sensitivity analysis. Infinite THs make far-future renewal emissions dominated by speculation (Resch).

5. Implications for extending C(T).
(i) Keep the year-cell structure, but make coefficients time-dependent: B(t) (grid mix, technology) and f(t) (occupancy, climate).
(ii) Represent each renewal event and the end-of-life residual as a process with zero time t_i0 and a normalized time function e_i(tau_i), so that the integral of e_i equals the static constant.
(iii) Build the inventory by convolution: deterministic or stochastic t_i0, delays and production periods.
(iv) Apply characterization as a second convolution evaluated at the study horizon T.
(v) Treat weighting and discounting separately.
(vi) Check the static limit and the integral identity, as in Pigné's Eq. 14.
results.open_questions:
1. Su, Li, Zhu, Lin 2017 (Energy and Buildings): the equations, and how each of the four dynamic properties is quantified, are UNCONFIRMED. The full text was blocked (LSU PDF behind a Cloudflare challenge; the ScienceDirect accepted manuscript returned 403). The same applies to Su, Li, Zhu 2019 (only the abstract was read) and to the ESPR 2021 review (only the abstract and a partial variable list via Slavkovic 2022). The 11 variables and 3 typical models of that review are unconfirmed. Su et al. 2021 (EIA Review 88:106568) is known only through Salati et al. 2025.
2. Collinge et al. 2013: the exact printed form of the dynamic equation, whether a weighting matrix W_t is included, the time step, and the erratum's content are UNCONFIRMED. The sum over t of C_t B_t A_t^-1 f_t comes from search-engine extracts and from Su et al. 2022's description of matrices C_t, B_t, A_t, f_t.
3. Fouquet et al. 2015: the candidate title 'Dynamic LCA of wood-based buildings' does not match; the actual title is 'Methodological challenges and developments in LCA of low energy buildings...'. The dynamic method, time horizon and lifetime are unconfirmed (abstract only).
4. Negishi 2018, the Negishi 2019 PhD and Negishi et al. 2019: full texts were blocked by HAL bot protection. The 12 building characteristics, the five-step method and the temporal-parameter database are unconfirmed beyond the abstracts and secondary mentions. The primary DyPLCA paper (Tiruta-Barna et al. 2016, J. Cleaner Production) was not read; its equations are taken from the Pigné et al. 2020 ESM summary.
5. 'Resch et al. review' and 'Morris et al. review': no review by either was found. Resch et al. 2021 (Building and Environment 187:107399) is a method and case paper. Morris, Allen and Hawkins 2021 (Building and Environment 206:108285) is a timber-versus-steel case study (search snippets only), not a review; I did not read it.
6. Not read; to check: Fnais et al. 2022 (Int J LCA, building LCA challenges); Elnour, Trigaux, Allacker, 'Dynamic life cycle assessment of building stocks: a systematic review' (venue unconfirmed); 'Time-explicit LCA' (Int J LCA 2025, doi 10.1007/s11367-025-02539-3); Sporchia, Schaubroeck, Pizzol (2026) matrix notation for temporal LCA (mentioned in search results; unconfirmed); Levasseur et al. 2010 (primary DCF source; only via Hoxha's reproduction); Collinge et al. 2018 ES&T (grid models; paywalled).
7. Hoxha et al. 2020, Eq. 5: the integration bounds (t_j to t), as reconstructed from the PDF text, may differ from Levasseur's per-time-step definition. This needs checking against Levasseur et al. 2010/2013 before adoption. Eq. 8's integration bounds are partly garbled.
8. Methodological gaps relevant to the chapter. No source read here writes building renewal cycles explicitly as process time functions with local times inside a time-dependent matrix and convolution formalism. Collinge and Su handle calendar-time matrices; DyPLCA handles supply-chain delays; Resch handles stochastic renewal times and separable tech and delay weights. A unified derivation is open.
9. Further open points: how to combine stochastic renewal times (chi-square in Resch, normal in Hosamo) with a deterministic convolution; how to keep GWP_T inventory data consistent with a dynamic horizon (Resch's limitation); and whether normalization and weighting should be dynamic at all (Sohn, Lueddeckens).

checks.citation: Negishi K, Tiruta-Barna L, Schiopu N, Lebert A, Chevalier J (2018). An operational methodology for applying dynamic Life Cycle Assessment to buildings. Building and Environment 144: 611-621.
checks.doi_ok: Correct. I checked Crossref: doi 10.1016/j.buildenv.2018.09.005 resolves to this title, these five authors, vol. 144, pp. 611-621, print date October 2018. The HAL API confirms hal-04335238 with the same DOI, vol. and pages; it is the author manuscript (28 pp, line-numbered), deposited 11 Dec 2023 under the HAL authorisation licence. I read the full text.
checks.equations_ok: Correct that there are none: the paper contains no equations. All quoted wording matches the manuscript: 'appears repeatedly in the life cycle system, but at different moments in time' (l. 509), construction '11 to 13 months [56]' (l. 543), 'renovation of floors occurs after 50 years' (l. 545), 'kg/day' (l. 546), 'partial or total integral of the flows over time' (l. 552), periods of '1 year, or 10 years' and 'the time scale is gridded' (l. 591-594), time zero 'can be placed anywhere' (l. 557), and 12% conductivity increase over 25 yr (l. 130). Table 2 has the six columns as listed.
checks.corrections:
Full text checked. Four points:
(1) Omission. The 2018 framework applies long-term energy-mix scenarios 'to both end-use energy consumption and energy consumption at the background processes of a building' (l. 587-589). The later case study (thesis 4.4.4 and Negishi et al. 2019) limits the mixes to end use. The survey does not record this difference.
(2) Precision. The paper says the SimaPro model 'includes many subsystems corresponding to periods'. After that, one technology matrix and one environmental-intervention matrix are generated and imported into DyPLCA (l. 590-599). So time dependence lives in a single static A and B that contain period-specific duplicate subsystems. 'Piecewise-constant A(t), B(t)' is the surveyor's interpretation, not the paper's wording.
(3) Ref. [56] for 11-13 months is Commissariat général au développement durable (2012). Ref. [48] is confirmed as Tiruta-Barna et al. 2016, J. Clean. Prod. 116:198-206.
(4) The DyPLCA URL printed in the paper is http://dyplca.pigne.org/. On 2026-11-14 its hostname did not resolve in DNS; the survey said only that it 'did not respond'.
Everything else in the entry is confirmed.

checks.citation: Tiruta-Barna L, Pigné Y, Navarrete Gutiérrez T, Benetto E (2016). Framework and computational tool for the consideration of time dependency in Life Cycle Inventory: proof of concept. Journal of Cleaner Production 116: 198-206.
checks.doi_ok: Correct. I checked Crossref: doi 10.1016/j.jclepro.2015.12.049, vol. 116, pp. 198-206, March 2016, same four authors. The HAL API shows hal-01886373 as a notice with no file, and OpenAlex reports it as closed access. Addition: the HAL record carries an external ISTEX full-text link that needs institutional access. I did not open it. So I read only the abstract, from the HAL API abstract_s field.
checks.equations_ok: No equations are claimed for this paper. I confirm that its equations, test bed and SI cannot be checked from open sources: unconfirmed. The abstract wording quoted in the survey is accurate, including 'representative functioning period, production time, supply delay, supply frequency', 'graph search algorithm ... prototype Web application' and 'solved both analytically and numerically'. Mapping these four parameters to T, r, delta and tau is an inference; it agrees with Pigné SI1 Table S1 and Shimako Table II.1.
checks.corrections:
Abstract only. Two points:
(1) Misattributed quote. The sentence quoted as the SI's argument ('an intrinsic dependence of the processes in the network ... a producer process will adapt its temporal characteristics ... which is not the case in a real-life scenario') is in the main text of Pigné et al. 2020 (p. 269). There it is written about the convolution approach of Beloin-Saint-Pierre et al. 2014 and Pinsonnault et al. 2014, and it ends '(for more information, see Tiruta-Barna et al. (2016) - supplementary information document)'. It is therefore a secondary statement by Pigné et al. What the 2016 SI itself argues is unconfirmed.
(2) Minor. The abstract's result types read '(i) time as a function of individual emission (or resource consumption) for individual processes, (ii) aggregated time as a function of a given environmental intervention'. The survey's paraphrase is fair.
The 'not confirmed from the original' caveats in the survey are appropriate and should stay.

checks.citation: Pigné Y, Navarrete Gutiérrez T, Gibon T, Schaubroeck T, Popovici E, Shimako AH, Benetto E, Tiruta-Barna L (2020). A tool to operationalize dynamic LCA, including time differentiation on the complete background database. Int J Life Cycle Assess 25(2): 267-279. With ESM1 (SI1).
checks.doi_ok: Correct. I checked Crossref: doi 10.1007/s11367-019-01696-6, vol. 25, issue 2, pp. 267-279, online 5 Nov 2019, print Feb 2020. The HAL API confirms hal-02353921 under CC BY 4.0. I read the full text from the HAL PDF, and SI1 from the Springer ESM docx at the URL given; I extracted its equations from the Word math objects.
checks.equations_ok:
All SI1 equations 1-15 match the docx: s = A^{-1} f; g = B s; a_{i,i} and b_{k,i} as integrals over [t0, t0+T]; sigma_{2,1} = max(floor(span_1/tau_{2,1}), 1); span_2 = tau_{2,1}(sigma_{2,1} - 1) + r_2; alpha_{2,1} = -(s_1 a_{2,1}/C_2(t)) alpha_{2,2}(t) and the matching beta; C_2(t) = sigma_{2,1} int_t^{t+r_2} alpha_{2,2} dt; C_2 = a_{2,2} span_1/T_2; the eq. 11 batch windows; the eq. 12 continuous window ending at t_{0,1} - r_2 - delta_2 + span_1 + r_2; g_{k,i,j} = int_{t_{0,i}}^{t_{0,f}+T_f} beta_{k,i,j} dt; g_k as a double sum; gamma_k = sum_i sum_j beta_{k,i,j}.
The main-text items also match: stop rule (a_{i,j} s_j times threshold), time limit, precision 'orders of magnitude lower than r', the printed discount factor '1/(1+year)x', 79% CO2 coverage at 1e-4 (EV, Fig. 4), and '>5 h' for 90% and 'almost nine full days' for 95%.
The survey's arithmetic checks are correct. For a constant alpha_{2,2} = a_{2,2}/T_2, eqs. 7, 10 and 12 deliver s_1|a_{2,1}|(1 + r_2/span_1). My own additional check: treating continuous supply as batches with tau = r_2, the last batch ends at t_{0,1} - delta_2 + (sigma - 1) r_2, which is about t_{0,1} - delta_2 + span_1 - r_2. So the eq. 12 upper bound overshoots by r_2, which supports the survey's point.
checks.corrections:
Full text and SI1 checked. Six points:
(1) Interpretation needs a caveat. The survey says eq. 11 is 'equivalent to convolving the producer's one-batch profile with a delayed Dirac pulse train'. That holds only when alpha_{2,2} is constant, or r-periodic with batch windows aligned to its phase. Calendar-dependent alpha is 'defined over 1 year, starting in January, regardless of whether the activity starts at another moment ... the specific activity intensity at that moment in time is considered' (Sect. 2.2.1(ii)). Eqs. 7 and 11 then evaluate alpha_{2,2} at absolute time inside each window. That is gating by indicator windows, not translation of one fixed batch shape. With an r-periodic alpha the integral in eq. 9 is still constant.
(2) Market processes are 'considered to occur instantaneously' with no temporal parameters, but with exceptions that do need temporal data. These are electricity markets that include transmission, and some fossil-fuel markets that include transport (natural gas, diesel) (Sect. 2.2.2).
(3) Internal inconsistency. The main text says cases are modelled in 'SimaPro or OpenLCA'. SI1 says import 'currently supports' only SimaPro CSV, and Sect. 4.3 lists OpenLCA compatibility as future work.
(4) SI1 also reports a jute-fibre test: threshold 1e-4 gives about 80% coverage in 8 min (Fig. S4-S5).
(5) Cosmetic. The SI1 text calls eqs. 7-8 'equation 5' and 'equation 6' (this also appears in Negishi's Annex I). Pigné's main text calls tau 'the frequency of a product supply', although SI1 Table S1 defines it as the interval between two supplies. The step-count sentence is ambiguous as printed ('span of the time horizon plus ... T divided by the step size'). Table 1 is per 1 vkm, uses a 100-yr window, and its caption prints the rate as 'of or 3%'.
(6) Tool check on 2026-11-14. http://dyplca.univ-lehavre.fr/ returned HTTP 503 (https gives a self-signed-certificate error). dyplca.pigne.org did not resolve in DNS.
All other assumptions and limits listed, including Table S7 rules, supply profiles, the IP-protected database and the attributional vs consequential t0 question, are confirmed.

checks.citation: Negishi K (2019). Development of a methodology of Dynamic LCA applied to the buildings (Développement d'une méthodologie d'ACV dynamique appliquée aux bâtiments). PhD thesis, INSA de Toulouse.
checks.doi_ok: Correct. The HAL record tel-02409097 is confirmed. Details the survey omitted: INSA de Toulouse, defended 21 June 2019, NNT 2019ISAT0013. HAL also assigns doi 10.70675/33bdcf34zae1cz4865za743z3212645986ef, which I confirmed redirects to theses.fr/2019ISAT0013. The PDF has 260 pages. I read the full text for the sections cited.
checks.equations_ok:
Confirmed:
- 'δ= -Y+r' is printed, with the example 'Construction product | Year 30' having δ = -31 (thesis p. 89, PDF p. 117).
- Fig. 4-6, checked as an image: process 2 spans [t0 - r2 - δ21, t0 - δ21], with T1 = r1, T2 = r2 and δ21 < 0.
- Building T = r = 50. Year-Y processes have T = r = 1 and alpha = 1/T. τ = Tc for single supply. Aggregators have δ = 0. 'Year 0' processes lie in year -1.
- Annex I eqs. (1)-(15) match Pigné SI1, except that eq. (6) is printed as span1 = τ2,1(σ2,1 - 1) + r2. The left-hand-side typo is confirmed.
- Eqs. 2-1 to 2-6 are as transcribed. 2-1 is printed with exp(-t/τ_k), and 2-6 reuses t as the inner variable.
- Table 4-6 gives +0.5%/yr, -1%/yr and -3%/yr, each relative to the preceding year.
The survey's reading that the worked example implies δ = -(Y + r) is arithmetically correct: with window [t0 - r - δ, t0 - δ], r = 1 and δ = -31 give [30, 31].
checks.corrections:
Full text checked for the cited sections. Five points:
(1) Product exclusion. 48 of 63 products were kept, so 15 were excluded, but under three criteria, not only the 1% rules: (i) GWP below 1%, (ii) inventory data completely lacking, (iii) mass below 1%. Exceptions: all insulation and heavy products were kept. The result is 98% of mass and 97% of GWP (Sect. 4.3.2.1).
(2) Technological progress is a '10% reduction every decade' of electricity consumption, applied to a few selected processes in aluminium, steel and concrete fabrication, including HVAC equipment replaced in use (Sect. 4.4.2).
(3) Eq. 2-4/2-5 symbols. The sum of the f_n is the climate sensitivity (K (W m-2)^-1). d_n (yr) is defined as 'the multiplication of the heat capacity of the system and the climate sensitivity'.
(4) Electricity mix. Sect. 4.4.4 gives the periods 2015-2034, 2035-2049 and 2050-2065, but Sect. 4.5.3.1 writes '2035-2050 and 2050-2065', an internal inconsistency. The first period uses the 2010 historical mix (72% nuclear). The two future scenarios are 'Mix-50% Nuclear' and 'Mix-90% RE&Gaz'.
(5) Tree growth is placed 'more than 100 years back from the construction' (p. ~90), which matches the survey.
The remaining open questions are fair: how year-specific degraded energy was encoded in DyPLCA, and the r of the aggregators. I found no explicit statement for either in the sections read.

checks.citation: Negishi K, Lebert A, Almeida D, Chevalier J, Tiruta-Barna L (2019). Evaluating climate change pathways through a building's lifecycle based on Dynamic Life Cycle Assessment. Building and Environment 164: 106377.
checks.doi_ok: Correct. Crossref, which the survey could not reach, now confirms doi 10.1016/j.buildenv.2019.106377: vol. 164, article number 106377, print date October 2019, same five authors. The HAL API confirms hal-02311410 under CC BY-NC 4.0 with page field '16 p.'. The HAL author manuscript PDF has 37 pages. I read the full text of sections 1-2.4 and parts of sections 3-4.
checks.equations_ok: No equations are claimed, which is correct. The numbers match: year 0 = 2015 = start of occupancy; 414 m2 over three houses; inventory from -150 to 51 yr; LCIA from -150 to 500 yr; results reported at 100 and 55 yr; 36.9 kWh m-2 yr-1 in the first year plus 20 kWh m-2 yr-1 for appliances; PVC window frames replaced at 30 yr (100% landfill) and disposed at 50 yr (92.1% landfill, 7.9% recycling); insulation replaced at 30 yr; Table 2 matches thesis Table 4-4, including 'just before the replacement/maintenance time t' and '0 < t < 50'.
checks.corrections:
Full text of the main sections checked. No substantive errors. Additions and refinements:
- The volume and article number are now Crossref-confirmed.
- The DyPLCA LCI was computed 'with a time step of 1 day' (l. 727-729). Hourly COMETH output was summed to yearly values for the LCI (l. 720-721).
- Scenarios vary one parameter each, except S6/sub-scenario 8 (l. 375-377).
- CO2 uptake into cement products is included when EPDs give it. Only carbonation after demolition is excluded (l. 295-298).
- 55 yr is described as 'the end time of the building system' (l. 411-412).
- Future mixes apply only to end-use energy (l. 370-372). This differs from the 2018 framework, which also applied them to background energy.
The SI tables (SI4, SI10, SI11) were not checked by me either: unconfirmed.

checks.citation: Shimako AH (2017). Contribution to the development of a dynamic Life Cycle Assessment method. PhD thesis, INSA de Toulouse.
checks.doi_ok: Correct. The HAL record tel-01706684 is confirmed. Details the survey omitted: INSA de Toulouse, defended 16 Nov 2017, NNT 2017ISAT0014. HAL also assigns doi 10.70675/0b11ef78z4080z48b7za371z9e44333da971, which redirects to theses.fr/2017ISAT0014. The PDF has 351 pages. I read the full text of Ch. II.2.
checks.equations_ok:
Confirmed in Ch. II, Sect. II.2.1 (pp. 30-32):
- Eq. II.3: t0^{l+1} = t0^l - r - δ.
- Eq. II.4: a_{l+1,l} = int_{t0}^{t0+T} φ_{l+1,l}(t) dt.
- Eqs. II.5 and II.6: α_{l+1,l} and β_{s,l+1,l} = -(s_l a_{l+1,l}/C_{l+1}) times the producer's own function. Both are printed with a stray trailing 'dt'; the survey noted this only for II.5.
- Eq. II.7: C_{l+1} = (T_l/τ_{l+1,l}) int_t^{t+r_{l+1}} α_{l+1,l+1}(t) dt.
- Eq. II.8: g_{s,l+1,l} = int_{t0i}^{t0f+Tf} β dt.
- Table II.1: 'τ=T for continuous supply'; δ = 'Storage time, no activity takes place'.
- 'breadth first search', and the mass-flow threshold plus backward time limit.
checks.corrections:
Full text checked for Ch. II.2. Four points:
(1) Equation numbering is ambiguous. The thesis also labels Chapter I equations 'Equation II.1'-'II.10' (s = As + f, s = (I - A)^{-1} f, g = Bs, and so on), so 'Eq. II.3' should be cited as Ch. II, Sect. II.2.1, p. 31.
(2) In Eq. II.3, r and δ carry no process index. Reading them as the producer's (level l+1) is an inference.
(3) The phrase 'more than 12 thousands activities' states the size of ecoinvent 3.2. Characterisation was done by ISIC class across working groups. It is not a statement that each activity was characterised individually.
(4) The DyPLCA URL given in this thesis is dyplca.univ-lehavre.fr. The thesis describes two tool versions: the first had no temporal database; the second added A/B import and the database.
The inconsistencies the survey notes between versions are confirmed: continuous τ = T here versus τ = r_producer in Pigné SI1, and T_l/τ here versus the integer σ in Pigné.

results.summary:
The survey holds up. All six sources exist and every citation, DOI and HAL record checks out.

I read everything from the primary sources:
- **Crossref** for all four journal DOIs. This now confirms Negishi et al. 2019, Building and Environment 164:106377 (October 2019), which the survey could not confirm.
- **HAL API** for all six records.
- **Full text** for Negishi et al. 2018 (HAL manuscript), Pigné et al. 2020 and its SI1 docx (equations taken from the Word math objects), the Negishi 2019 thesis (cited sections, Annex I, and Fig. 4-6 checked as an image), Negishi et al. 2019 (sections 1-2.4 plus parts of 3-4) and the Shimako 2017 thesis (Ch. II.2).
- **Abstract only** for Tiruta-Barna et al. 2016. It is closed access; the HAL record links to an ISTEX copy that needs institutional access, and I did not open it. Its equations, test bed and supplementary information remain unconfirmed.

All equations the survey transcribes match the sources, including its claimed typos:
- thesis Annex I eq. 6 printed with span1 on the left;
- thesis p. 89 printing 'δ= -Y+r' next to the example δ = -31 (the example implies -(Y + r));
- Pigné's discount factor printed as '1/(1+year)x'.

The surveyor's two arithmetic checks are also correct: the continuous-supply total is off by a factor (1 + r2/span1), and sigma = floor(50/30) = 1.

**Corrections, most important first:**
1. **Misattributed quote.** The "intrinsic dependence ... producer process will adapt ..." sentence is in the main text of Pigné et al. 2020 (p. 269), written about the convolution approach of Beloin-Saint-Pierre et al. 2014. It only refers readers to the 2016 supplementary information; it is not a quote from it.
2. **Convolution reading needs a limit.** Reading SI1 eq. 11 as "the producer's one-batch profile convolved with a pulse train" only works when the production function is constant or its cycles line up with the batches. For calendar-dependent functions (defined from January), the paper evaluates them at absolute time. That is gating by time windows, not shifting one fixed shape.
3. **Negishi et al. 2018 applies the future energy mix to background processes too**, not just end use (l. 587-589). The 2019 case study narrows it to end use only. The survey misses this difference.
4. **Pigné et al. 2020 contradicts itself on software.** The main text says SimaPro or OpenLCA; SI1 import supports only SimaPro CSV, and the paper lists OpenLCA support as future work. Market processes also have exceptions (electricity transmission, gas and diesel markets) that do need time parameters.
5. **Negishi thesis details:**
   - The 15 excluded products fall under three rules (1% of GWP, missing data, 1% of mass), not just the 1% rules.
   - Technology progress is a 10% cut per decade in *electricity* use for a few selected processes.
   - The thesis gives the electricity-mix periods inconsistently between sections 4.4.4 and 4.5.3.1.
   - d_n is defined as heat capacity times climate sensitivity.
6. **Shimako thesis:** equation numbers II.1-II.10 are also used in Chapter I, so cite the formulas as Ch. II, Sect. II.2.1, pp. 30-32. "More than 12 thousands activities" describes the size of ecoinvent 3.2, not how many were characterised.
7. **Small additions:**
   - Thesis DOIs and NNTs: 2019ISAT0013 and 2017ISAT0014; both DOIs resolve to theses.fr.
   - Negishi et al. 2019 ran DyPLCA with a 1-day time step.
   - Pigné SI1 also reports a jute test: about 80% coverage at threshold 1e-4 in 8 minutes.
   - Tool check on 2026-11-14: dyplca.univ-lehavre.fr returns HTTP 503, and the https version fails on a self-signed certificate. dyplca.pigne.org does not resolve in DNS at all, rather than just not responding.

Downloaded copies are in <local copy> and the extracted text in <local copy>

results.topic: Dynamic characterization and time horizons for the climate impact of building emissions: DCF(t), the CO2 impulse response, fixed calendar endpoint vs fixed horizon per emission, convolving an emission timeline e(t) with the response, and the assumptions behind it (linearity, constant background, constant radiative efficiency). Purpose: extending a building whole-life-carbon C(T) into a dynamic LCA.

sources.citation: Levasseur A, Lesage P, Margni M, Deschênes L, Samson R (2010) Considering time in LCA: dynamic LCA and its application to global warming impact assessments. Environmental Science & Technology 44(8):3169-3174
sources.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1021/es9030003 (ACS returned 403; Semantic Scholar lists it as CLOSED access; the PolyPublie record https://publications.polymtl.ca/17984/ and A. Levasseur's 2011 thesis https://publications.polymtl.ca/706/1/2011_AnnieLevasseur.pdf both returned HTTP 503)

equations.expression: DCF_i(t)_cumulative = AGWP_i(t) = \int_0^t a_i [C_i(t)] dt
equations.symbols: From Breton et al. 2018, Eq. 2, citing L2010. C_i(t) = residual atmospheric concentration of GHG i after a pulse emission (kg kg^-1). a_i = radiative efficiency, i.e. instantaneous radiative forcing per unit mass increase in the atmosphere (W m^-2 kg^-1). t = years since the emission.
equations.meaning: Breton quotes L2010 for the DCF: 'the cumulative radiative forcing per unit mass of GHG released in the atmosphere since the emission' (W yr m^-2 kg^-1). Equals the AGWP integrated up to t.

equations.expression: DCF_i(t)_instantaneous = \int_{t-1}^{t} a_i [C_i(t)] dt
equations.symbols: As above. The time axis is cut into one-year increments.
equations.meaning: The yearly DCF: forcing integrated over year t after a unit pulse (Breton Eq. 3). Heijungs 2026 gives the same form as his Eq. 17.

equations.expression: GWI_inst(t) = \sum_i GWI_i(t) = \sum_i \sum_{j=0}^{t} [g_i]_j \cdot [DCF_i]_{t-j}
equations.symbols: [g_i]_j = dynamic LCI result (mass of GHG i emitted) in year j. [DCF_i]_{t-j} = yearly DCF of GHG i at lag t-j. t = calendar year counted from the start of the life cycle.
equations.meaning: A discrete convolution of the emission timeline with the yearly DCF kernel. This is what the user's framework calls local time tau = t - t_j0. Breton gives the unit as 'W yr m^-2' and Heijungs notes that the units are inconsistent.

equations.expression: GWI_cum(t) = \sum_{j=0}^{t} GWI_inst(j)
equations.symbols: GWI_inst from the equation above.
equations.meaning: Cumulative global warming impact up to calendar year t. Breton attributes this form to Levasseur et al. 2012/2013 (J Ind Ecol), not to L2010.

equations.symbols: t in years. These are the AR4 (Bern2.5CC) coefficients.
equations.meaning: The CO2 IRF used with L2010, as reproduced by Heijungs 2026 (his Eq. 18). The Ventura & Feraille 2021 note gives the same a_i values as the 'IPCC AR4 model' basis of RE2020.

equations.expression: C_i(t) = e^{-t/\tau_i}, \tau_{CH4} = 12 yr, \tau_{N2O} = 114 yr
equations.symbols: tau_i = perturbation lifetime.
equations.meaning: Single-exponential decay for gases other than CO2. Heijungs says L2010 gives no tau values and takes them from Solomon et al. 2007.

sources.assumptions: Per the abstract (paraphrase via the ETS portal): first a dynamic LCI with the temporal profile of emissions, then time-dependent characterization factors giving 'real-time impact scores for any given time horizon', built on radiative forcing. The time horizon is a fixed calendar endpoint. Breton (Fig. 3, adapted from L2010) shows a 75-year building life cycle inside a 100-year assessment period. Heijungs quotes L2010 calling this a 'flexible time horizon' needed 'to be consistent with the 100-year time horizon chosen for the analysis'. Heijungs also says L2010 takes t = 0 as 'the beginning of the life cycle'.
sources.conditions_and_limits: I did not read the full text. All equations above come from Breton 2018 and Heijungs 2026, not from L2010 itself. Heijungs reports that L2010 defines an instantaneous and a cumulative DCF but convolves with a third, undefined [DCF_i]_{t-j}, gives no a_i or tau values, gives no DCF table, and has typos. He also says Levasseur et al. (2012a) 'corrected this mistake'. L2010's own equation numbering is unconfirmed: my two fetch summaries of Heijungs disagree on it. Emissions or forcing after the endpoint are excluded.
sources.relevance: This is the core template for the user's e_i(t) convolved with a kernel. Process time functions e_i(t) map to [g_i]_j, local time tau_i = t - t_i0 maps to the lag t - j, and DCF_i(tau) is the kernel. The building C(T) at a fixed calendar endpoint T maps to GWI_cum(T), with constants at t = 0, year cells as annual g_i, renewal events at t_k, and the end-of-life residual at the end of the study period.
sources.time_variables: t = calendar year from the start of the life cycle (t = 0). j = emission year. t - j = time since emission. The time step is one year. TH = fixed calendar endpoint of the analysis (e.g. 100 years).

sources.citation: Kendall A (2012) Time-adjusted global warming potentials for LCA and carbon footprints. International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment 17:1042-1049
sources.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11367-012-0436-5 (read from the copy hosted by CARB: https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/classic/fuels/lcfs/workshops/04302019_its-davis_kendallarticle.pdf)

equations.expression: GWP_{AT} = \int_0^{AT} RF_i dt / \int_0^{AT} RF_{CO2} dt = CRF_i / CRF_{CO2}
equations.symbols: AT = analytical time horizon. RF = radiative forcing, a function of a gas's decay rate and its radiative efficiency. i = the GHG converted into CO2e. CRF = cumulative radiative forcing.
equations.meaning: Eq. 1: the conventional GWP.

equations.expression: TAWP = \int_0^{AT-y} RF_i(t) dt / \int_0^{AT} RF_{CO2}(t) dt
equations.symbols: y = years in the future that the emission occurs, so it is in the atmosphere for AT - y years at the end of AT. The reference gas is CO2 and the reference time is year 0 (today).
equations.meaning: Eq. 2: time-adjusted warming potential. Only the numerator's integration limit moves, so the result is in 'CO2 equivalent today'.

equations.expression: CO2e = mass of emission_i \times TAWP_{AT}(y)
equations.symbols: TAWP_AT(y) from Eq. 2.
equations.meaning: Eq. 3: TAWPs are applied like GWPs, per emission year.

sources.assumptions: The CRF model uses IPCC AR4 lifetimes, radiative efficiencies and indirect effects (methane only), cited as 'IPCC 2011', plus the AGWP methods of Shine et al. 2005. CO2 is the reference gas and t = 0 is today. In the building case all CO2e is treated as CO2.
sources.conditions_and_limits: Kendall names the trade-off explicitly. A metric with a fixed future point in time (like the TAWP) favours 'pushing emissions into the future'. A metric that evaluates every emission over identical periods (GWP) loses the endpoint information. She calls this an 'unavoidable trade-off'. Forcing after the horizon gets zero value. Limited significant digits make the TAWP at y = 0 differ slightly from IPCC GWPs (e.g. 0.08 kg for CH4 at 500 years). Short-lived climate forcers are excluded. The best-fit polynomials and the TAWPv1.0 tool are in the supplementary material, which I did not read. Table 1 (1 kg emitted at year 10, in kg CO2e today) for AT = 20/30/50/100/500: CO2 0.578/0.739/0.855/0.930/0.987; CH4 52.4/53.3/42.0/25.4/7.68; N2O 158/214/261/281/154.
sources.relevance: Building case (after Scheuer et al. 2003): a commercial building with 135,000 t CO2e over 75 years, split as 4,360.5 t at year 0, 1,737.5 t per year for 75 years, and 324 t at decommissioning. TAWP100 gives 93,315 t CO2e (more than 30 % lower than simple summation). TAWP500 gives 127,591 t and PAS 2050 'general case' gives 83,884 t. The paper text says '93,315 kg' once while Table 2 is in t CO2e. This is exactly the constants + year cells + EoL-residual structure of C(T). TAWP equals the fixed-endpoint convolution normalised by AGWP_CO2(AT).
sources.time_variables: y = emission year after the reference time 0. AT = analytical horizon, measured from year 0 (a fixed calendar endpoint). Integration runs over AT - y for each emission.

sources.citation: Joos F, Roth R, Fuglestvedt JS, Peters GP, Enting IG, von Bloh W, Brovkin V, et al. (2013) Carbon dioxide and climate impulse response functions for the computation of greenhouse gas metrics: a multi-model analysis. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 13:2793-2825

equations.expression: AGWP_x(TH) = \int_0^{TH} RF_x(t) dt = \int_0^{TH} A_x \cdot IRF_x(t) dt ;  GWP_x(TH) = AGWP_x(TH)/AGWP_{CO2}(TH)
equations.symbols: RF_x(t) = radiative forcing at time t from a pulse released at t = 0. A_x = radiative forcing per kg increase in atmospheric burden. IRF_x(t) = fraction of the added pulse still in the atmosphere at time t. TH = time horizon.
equations.meaning: Eqs. 1-2: AGWP and GWP.

equations.expression: RF_{CO2}(\Delta N_{CO2}) = 5.35 W m^{-2} \ln((N_{CO2,0} + \Delta N_{CO2})/N_{CO2,0}) ;  small \Delta N:  RF = 5.35 W m^{-2} \Delta N_{CO2}/N_{CO2,0} = A_{CO2} \Delta N_{CO2}
equations.symbols: N_CO2,0 = reference burden. Delta N_CO2 = perturbation.
equations.meaning: Eqs. 3-4, after Myhre et al. 1998. In the small-perturbation limit A_CO2 is constant and time-invariant.

equations.expression: IRF_x(t) = a_{x,0} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{x,i} \exp(-t/\tau_{x,i}),  t \ge 0
equations.symbols: a_x,i = unitless fractions that sum to 1. a_x,0 = fraction that stays permanently. tau_x,i = nominal timescales, which for CO2 are fitting parameters with no process meaning.
equations.meaning: Eq. 5: the sum-of-exponentials IRF.

equations.expression: AGWP_x(TH) = A_x a_{x,0} TH + A_x \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{x,i} \tau_{x,i} (1 - \exp(-TH/\tau_{x,i}))
equations.symbols: As above.
equations.meaning: Eq. 6: closed-form AGWP, which is the analytic DCF_cumulative.

equations.expression: CO2(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} e(t') \cdot IRF_{CO2}(t - t') dt' + CO2(t_0)
equations.symbols: e(t') = anthropogenic emissions at t'. t_0 = a time of approximate steady state.
equations.meaning: Eq. 7: the change in atmospheric CO2 is the convolution of the emission timeline with the IRF. Joos calls this valid 'in a linear approximation'.

equations.symbols: From Table 5 (fit by Eq. 11 to the multi-model mean). The setup is a 100 GtC pulse into a constant 389 ppm background (PD100). The mean relative error of the fit is 0.6 %.
equations.meaning: The recommended multi-model-mean CO2 IRF: 'We suggest to use numerical values as obtained by these fits for the multi-model mean in future studies.'

equations.symbols: Uses a 389 ppm background and the 2.123 GtC per ppm conversion.
equations.meaning: The CO2 radiative efficiency per kg used for AGWP_CO2. The abstract gives a best-estimate AGWP_CO2(100) of 92.5e-15 yr W m^-2 per kg CO2 (68 to 117 at 5-95 %).

equations.expression: AGTP_x(TH) = \Delta T(TH) / e_x(t=0)
equations.symbols: Delta T = global-mean surface temperature change at TH after a unit pulse e_x at t = 0.
equations.meaning: Eq. 8: AGTP is the temperature impulse response.

sources.assumptions: Joos states: 'For sufficiently small emissions and approximately constant background conditions the radiative efficiency, A_x, can be approximated as time-invariant.' IRFs fully characterize a linear system. AR4 GWPs relied on the Bern2.5CC model.
sources.conditions_and_limits: 'The IRF_CO2 is not an invariant function, but depends on the magnitude of the carbon emissions.' Non-linearities come from carbonate chemistry, circulation change and terrestrial feedbacks, which 'limit the accuracy of the above equation substantially'. The IRF and AGWP depend on background concentration, pulse size and model. The time-integrated IRF is about 23 % lower under pre-industrial than present-day conditions, while forcing per unit CO2 is 39 % higher, so integrated forcing is nearly unchanged. Under RCP backgrounds (Bern3D-LPJ) the time-integrated IRF at year 100 is 66/68/69/75 yr for RCP2.6/4.5/6.0/8.5, versus 62 yr for the 389 ppm case. Under RCP8.5 more than 80 % of the pulse is still airborne at year 1000. The fit is valid only from 0 to 1000 years. Integrated IRF from the fit is 14.2/30.3/52.4/184/310 yr at 20/50/100/500/1000 years.
sources.relevance: This supplies the kernel C_CO2(tau) and the closed-form DCF_cum(tau) for the dynamic C(T). Eq. 7 is the continuous form of the user's convolution e_i(t) * response(tau). The background-dependence results quantify the error of a time-invariant kernel for building emissions released decades ahead (e.g. EoL around 2075).
sources.time_variables: t = years after the pulse (local time). t' = emission time. TH = horizon measured from each pulse, i.e. a per-emission horizon in the metric definition.

sources.citation: Cherubini F, Peters GP, Berntsen T, Strømman AH, Hertwich E (2011) CO2 emissions from biomass combustion for bioenergy: atmospheric decay and contribution to global warming. GCB Bioenergy 3(5):413-426
sources.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1757-1707.2011.01102.x (Crossref metadata confirmed. Green OA copy at http://hdl.handle.net/11250/2468351, but the NTNU/NVA repository returned empty pages and Wiley returned 403.)

equations.expression: f(t) = \int_0^t [C_0 e(t') - C_0^* NEP(t')] y_{CO2}(t - t') dt'
equations.symbols: From Breton et al. 2018, Eq. 6, citing Guest et al. and Cherubini. e(t) = distributed emission profile of the product (e.g. Gaussian, Dirac delta, Gamma, chi-square), including temporary storage. NEP(t) = net ecosystem productivity of the biomass source (NPP minus heterotrophic respiration). Both are normalised to the unit emission profile. y(t) = CO2 IRF of the carbon-cycle climate model. C_0 and C_0* = scaling factors for emission and removal; C_0* = 1 means carbon-neutral regrowth.
equations.meaning: The biogenic atmospheric decay function, built by convolving the product emission minus regrowth with the fossil CO2 IRF. The bracket placement is my reconstruction from garbled PDF text.

equations.expression: GWP_{bio} = AGWP_{bioCO2}/AGWP_{CO2} = C_0 \int_0^{TH} \alpha_{CO2} f(t) dt / ( C_0 \int_0^{TH} \alpha_{CO2} y(t) dt )
equations.symbols: alpha = radiative efficiency (W m^-2 kg^-1). f(t) = biogenic IRF. y(t) = fossil CO2 IRF. TH = time horizon.
equations.meaning: Breton Eq. 7. The factor multiplies direct biogenic CO2 emissions to give kg CO2-eq. Breton says GWPbio uses a fixed endpoint for TH.

sources.assumptions: Abstract (paraphrased via Semantic Scholar): CO2 IRFs from carbon-cycle models are used to build atmospheric decay functions for biomass-derived CO2. The unit-based index GWPbio depends on the rotation period. Assuming climate neutrality for flux-neutral bioenergy underestimates the impact. Per Breton, there is possible small double counting of vegetation sinks, except for carbon-cycle models without forest management.
sources.conditions_and_limits: I did not read the primary text. The y(t) parameters (Bern carbon-cycle model version), the regrowth function g(t) and the GWPbio tables are unconfirmed.
sources.relevance: Shows a static-LCI alternative: the convolution is moved into the characterization factor for one process (e.g. a timber element with rotation, storage and EoL release). By linearity, several replacement cycles of one product can be combined into one e(t) (Breton).
sources.time_variables: t = time since the reference emission. t' = integration variable. Rotation period. TH = fixed endpoint.

sources.citation: Breton C, Blanchet P, Amor B, Beauregard R, Chang W-S (2018) Assessing the climate change impacts of biogenic carbon in buildings: a critical review of two main dynamic approaches. Sustainability 10(6):2020

equations.expression: DCF_i(t)_cum = AGWP_i(t) = \int_0^t a_i[C_i(t)]dt ; DCF_i(t)_inst = \int_{t-1}^{t} a_i[C_i(t)]dt ; GWI_inst(t) = \sum_i \sum_{j=0}^{t} [g_i]_j [DCF_i]_{t-j} ; GWI_cum(t) = \sum_{j=0}^{t} GWI_inst(j)
equations.symbols: See the Levasseur 2010 entry. Breton gives the CO2 radiative efficiency (from Myhre et al. 2013 SM, at 391 ppm) as 1.7517e-15 W m^-2 kg^-1. For CO2 he recommends the multi-model average IRF of Joos et al. 2013.
equations.meaning: Breton Eqs. 2-5: the DLCA framework.

equations.expression: f(t) = \int_0^t [C_0 e(t') - C_0^* NEP(t')] y_{CO2}(t-t') dt' ;  GWP_{bio} = \int_0^{TH}\alpha f dt / \int_0^{TH}\alpha y dt
equations.symbols: See the Cherubini 2011 entry.
equations.meaning: Breton Eqs. 6-7: GWPbio.

sources.assumptions: From the text: IRFs 'can fully describe the response of linear and time-invariant systems'. 'The carbon cycle-climate systems are nonlinear, and the IRF for CO2 is not invariant, but varies with the magnitude of the carbon emissions.' However, 'for sufficiently small CO2 emission pulses (<100 GtC) with approximate constant background concentrations, the IRF is found to be linear'. The Table 6 results assume constant background CO2 emissions.
sources.conditions_and_limits: Terminology warning: Breton calls a horizon counted from each emission a 'fixed time horizon (sliding window)' and a calendar endpoint a 'variable time horizon (fixed endpoint)'. Under a fixed endpoint, early emissions get longer horizons, impacts after the endpoint are excluded, and results are more sensitive to TH. Pushing emissions later lowers impacts, and pushing them past the assessment period removes them, which 'infringes the intergenerational equity concept'. Breton therefore requires sensitivity analysis across short, mid and long TH and reporting of later emissions as a memo item. Applying GWPbio only to biogenic flows mixes fixed-endpoint and sliding-horizon metrics and partly reintroduces the inconsistency. Table 6 (GWP20/GWP100/GTP20/GTP100): pulse 1/1/1/1; concentrated (Gamma, 95 % within 5 years) 0.91/0.98/0.99/1.00; distributed (chi-square around year 75, 70-year rotation) 0.16/-0.23/0.18/0.06.
sources.relevance: This is the building-specific bridge. Breton's Fig. 3 (75-year building inside a 100-year assessment period) is the C(T) study-period setting. Breton notes DLCA combines dynamic LCI and DCF 'by using a matrix approach'. He cites ESPA (Beloin-Saint-Pierre) for deriving dynamic LCIs by convolution, and Temporalis (Brightway2) and DYNCO2 as tools. Replacement events can be merged into one emission profile by linearity.
sources.time_variables: Three time notions (after Brandão et al.): the characterization time horizon, the period of assessment, and the life cycle. t = calendar year from t = 0. j = emission year. TH = fixed endpoint.

sources.citation: Ventura A (2023; online 15 Feb 2022) Conceptual issue of the dynamic GWP indicator and solution. International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment 28:788-799
sources.doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11367-022-02028-x (Springer page shows abstract and preview only; not open access)

equations.expression: TOD = LCD + THI
equations.symbols: TOD = Time of Observation Duration. LCD = life cycle duration. THI = Time Horizon of the Impact.
equations.meaning: Stated in the visible text as the total observation duration for any dynamic approach.

equations.expression: L2010 as rendered by Ventura (per Heijungs 2026, Eq. 50):  \sum_x\sum_i \int_{t_i}^{TOD} a_x C_x(t-t_i) dt / \int_{?}^{TOD} a_{CO2} C_{CO2}(t) dt
equations.symbols: x = GHG. t_i = emission time. TOD is fixed and 'commonly chosen' as 100 years.
equations.meaning: The fixed-calendar-endpoint dynamic GWP. The lower limit of the denominator is unconfirmed: the fetch tool transcribed it as t_i, while Ventura & Feraille 2021 (Eq. 6) integrate the denominator from 0.

equations.expression: Ventura's modification (per Heijungs 2026, Eq. 51):  \sum_x\sum_i \int_{t_i}^{t_i+THI} a_x C_x(t-t_i) dt / \int_0^{t_i+THI} a_{CO2} C_{CO2}(t) dt
equations.symbols: THI = fixed horizon of impact applied after each emission.
equations.meaning: Each emission is integrated over exactly THI. The reference CO2 pulse at t = 0 is integrated to t_i + THI. This matches Eq. 9 of Ventura & Feraille 2021.

sources.assumptions: Three 'basic principles' (abstract/preview): (1) no inventory flow may be omitted; (2) all substances in a category share the same THI; (3) THI does not change as a function of time.
sources.conditions_and_limits: Per the abstract, the initial (L2010) indicator overestimates the effect of temporary carbon storage by about 25 % at 50 years, and the corrected method can be implemented in RE2020 by changing only the FRE2020(t) coefficients. Heijungs 2026 judges that Ventura's version still mixes the characterization factor with the indicator and reintroduces a CO2 reference. Equations are known to me only through secondary renderings.
sources.relevance: This is the 'fixed horizon after each emission' option. For C(T), each event m_k at t_k would get the weight AGWP_g(THI)/AGWP_CO2(t_k + THI), with no truncation by the study period.
sources.time_variables: t_i = emission time. THI = per-emission horizon. LCD = life-cycle duration. TOD = total observation duration = LCD + THI.

sources.citation: Ventura A, Feraille A (2021) Recommandations pour l'introduction de l'Analyse de Cycle de Vie (ACV) dans la Réglementation Environnementale (RE) 2020 des bâtiments. Note, Université Gustave Eiffel / ENPC, version 2, 22 March 2021 (grey literature, addressed to the French ministry DGALN/DHUP)

equations.expression: prg_x = \int_0^{HTI} a_x(t)[x(t)] dt / \int_0^{HTI} a_r(t)[r(t)] dt
equations.symbols: HTI = time horizon of the impact. t = 0 = emission instant. a_x(t), a_r(t) = radiative efficiency of gas x and of reference CO2 (W m^-2 kg^-1). [x(t)], [r(t)] = residual mass from 1 kg emitted at t = 0.
equations.meaning: Eq. 1: the static GWP.

equations.symbols: The extracted text prints tau_1 = '1 729 ans' and tau_3 = '1 186 ans'. These look like 172.9 and 1.186 with the decimal separators lost (the AR4 values Heijungs reproduces), but that is unconfirmed.
equations.meaning: Eq. 2: the AR4 CO2 decay that underlies RE2020 dynamic LCA.

equations.expression: PRG_dyn^{HTI} = \sum_i [\int_{t_i}^{t_i+HTI} a_{x_i}[x(t-t_i)]dt / \int_{t_i}^{t_i+HTI} a_r[r(t-t_i)]dt] m_i
equations.symbols: m_i = mass emitted at t_i.
equations.meaning: Eq. 5: a horizon that slides with each emission and uses its own reference. It is strictly equal to the static indicator for the same HTI and only adds the time detail.

equations.expression: \Delta PRG_dyn^{DO} = \sum_i [\int_{t_i}^{DO} a_{x_i}[x(t-t_i)]dt / \int_0^{DO} a_r[r(t)]dt] m_i
equations.symbols: DO = fixed observation duration (100 years in RE2020).
equations.meaning: Eq. 6: the Levasseur/CIRAIG fixed-calendar-endpoint dynamic indicator on which RE2020 is based.

equations.expression: 0 \le t_i \le 50: \Delta PRG_{dyn,simpl} = \sum_i (1 - 0.00842 t_i) prg_{x_i} m_i ;  t_i \le 0: \sum_i prg_{x_i} m_i ;  t_i \ge 50: \sum_i (1 - 0.00842\cdot 50) prg_{x_i} m_i ;  as a function of T: \sum_i (1-0.00842 t_i) prg_{x_i} H(T-t_i) m_i
equations.symbols: t_i = years since construction (t = 0). H = Heaviside step. 0.00842 per year is the note authors' linear-regression estimate from the RE2020 Excel file, not an official value. The text also writes 0.00845 once.
equations.meaning: Eq. 7/7T: the RE2020 simplified dynamic method. It is calibrated to match Eq. 6 with DO = 100 years. Emissions before t = 0 are static and emissions after 50 years are clamped to year 50.

equations.expression: DO(t) = t + HTI ;  \Delta PRG_{dyn,corr} = \sum_i [\int_{t_i}^{t_i+HTI} a_{x_i}[x(t-t_i)]dt / \int_0^{t_i+HTI} a_r[r(t)]dt] m_i
equations.symbols: HTI = 100 years for every emission.
equations.meaning: Eqs. 8-9: the corrected method. For a 50-year building and HTI = 100 the observation duration spans 100-150 years. Corrected coefficients: t = 0 gives 1.0000, 10 gives 0.9258, 25 gives 0.8350, 50 gives 0.7211 (RE2020 gives 0.58 at 50 years), so RE2020 overstates the reduction by about 35 %.

sources.assumptions: Radiative efficiencies are held constant between IPCC updates. RE2020 puts t = 0 at construction, treats pre-construction emissions as static, and sets life-cycle duration = service life = 50 years. The note's RE table (W m^-2 ppb^-1, for 2001/2007/2013/2016): CO2 1.55e-5/1.4e-5/1.37e-5/1.53e-5; CH4 3.7e-4/3.7e-4/3.63e-4/4.48e-4; N2O 3.1e-3/3.03e-3/3.03e-3/2.67e-3. The note's text elsewhere gives CH4 as 3.4e-4 for 2007, which is inconsistent with its own table.
sources.conditions_and_limits: 'No dynamic method today accounts for the time variation of radiative efficiency.' Future values depend on mitigation, and delayed emissions in a high-emission future could be worse. Delaying emissions by a few decades is negligible over the long term. Worked example (1 kg CO2 every 25 years, 5 times): with DO = 100 the reduction versus static is 2.23 kg CO2-eq (44.6 %); with DO corrected to 200 it is 1.04 kg (20.8 %). The note says DCV (life-cycle duration) should span first extraction to last waste emission (e.g. 50 years before construction for timber, 50 years after demolition). The fixed t = 0 penalises long pre-construction delays and reuse.
sources.relevance: This is the most direct building C(T) analogue: a regulatory year-weight w(t_i) multiplying static GWP per emission year, which is a first-order discrete kernel. It lays out the static, sliding, fixed-endpoint and fixed-HTI conventions side by side with the same symbols.
sources.time_variables: t_i = emission year since construction. HTI = impact horizon. DO = observation duration. DCV = life-cycle duration. DVP = product service life. T = integration or observation time.

sources.citation: Heijungs R (2026) Dynamic characterization factors and dynamic global warming potentials: a critical methodological review. International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment 31: article 64

equations.expression: RF_i(t) = RE_i \cdot C_i(t) ;  AGWP_{i,T} = \int_0^T RF_i(t) dt ;  AGTP_{i,T} = \int_0^T RF_i(t) R(T-t) dt
equations.symbols: RE_i = radiative efficiency. C_i(t) = atmospheric load after a pulse. R = temperature response function (after Fuglestvedt et al. 2010).

equations.expression: h_T = \sum_i \sum_{t=0}^{T} q_i(T-t) g_i(t)
equations.symbols: g_i(t) = emission of i at time t. q_i = characterization kernel at lag T - t.
equations.meaning: Eq. 12: the dynamic characterization result written explicitly as a discrete convolution.

equations.expression: DCF_i(t)_{cum} = \sum_{t'=1}^{t} DCF_i(t')_{inst} = \int_0^t a_i C_i(k) dk ;  GWI_T = \sum_i \sum_{t=0}^{T} DCF_i(T-t)_{inst} g_i(t) ;  GWI_T \overset{?}{=} \sum_i\sum_{t=0}^{T} DCF_i(T-t)_{cum} g_i(t)
equations.symbols: As in L2010.
equations.meaning: Eqs. 15, 21, 23, 25: the reconstruction of L2010. Heijungs marks the identifications in Eqs. 16 and 23 as speculative ('?').

equations.expression: GWI_inst(t) = \sum_{j=0}^{t} [g_i]_j [DCF_i]_{t-j} ;  GWI_cum(T) = \sum_{t=0}^{T}\sum_{j=0}^{t} g_i(j) DCF_i(t-j) ;  DCF_{inst,CO2}(t-t_j) = \int_{t_j}^{t} A_{CO2} C_{CO2}(t) dt
equations.symbols: Notation as attributed to follow-up papers (Ghannadzadeh & Van der Meer; Saade et al.).
equations.meaning: Eqs. 47-49: variant forms of the same convolution found in the literature.

results.synthesis:
1. Common structure: a convolution. Every method surveyed computes a linear, time-invariant convolution of a dynamic inventory with a pulse-response kernel.
- Continuous form (Joos 2013, Eq. 7): DeltaCO2(t) = int e(t') IRF(t - t') dt'.
- Forcing: RF_g(t) = a_g * int e_g(t') C_g(t - t') dt'.
- Cumulative forcing at calendar time T: CRF(T) = sum_g int_0^T e_g(t') AGWP_g(T - t') dt'. This uses AGWP_g(s) = DCF_g,cum(s) = A_g[a0 s + sum a_i tau_i (1 - e^(-s/tau_i))] (Joos Eq. 6).
- Discrete forms: L2010's GWI_inst(t) = sum_i sum_j [g_i]_j [DCF_i]_{t-j}, and Heijungs' h_T = sum_i sum_t q_i(T - t) g_i(t).
- Mapping onto the user's framework: process time function e_i(t) = g_i(t); local time tau_i = t - t_i0 = the lag argument of C, DCF or AGWP; the kernel is a_g C_g(tau).
- A temperature layer adds a second convolution with R_theta: AGTP = a int c(t) R(T - t) dt (Joos Eq. 8, Heijungs Eq. 10, François Eqs. 5 and 17).

2. Kernels as cited.
- CO2 (AR4/Bern2.5CC, used by L2010, DYNCO2, Kendall and RE2020): 0.217 + 0.259e^(-t/172.9) + 0.338e^(-t/18.51) + 0.186e^(-t/1.186).
- CO2 (Joos 2013 multi-model mean, 100 GtC into 389 ppm, valid 0-1000 yr; also used in the AR6-labelled Brightway code): 0.2173 + 0.2240e^(-t/394.4) + 0.2824e^(-t/36.54) + 0.2763e^(-t/4.304). The integral to 100 years is 52.4 yr.
- A_CO2 = 1.77e-15 W m^-2 kg^-1 (Joos, 389 ppm). Breton cites 1.7517e-15 at 391 ppm (AR5).
- Non-CO2 gases: e^(-t/tau) (CH4 12 yr and N2O 114 yr in the AR4-based reconstructions).

3. Horizon conventions. This is the central modelling choice for C(T), and the literature uses opposite names for the same thing: Breton calls a horizon counted from each emission 'fixed time horizon (sliding window)' and a calendar endpoint 'variable time horizon (fixed endpoint)'. For an emission at t_i:
- (a) Static/sliding: integrate over THI with the reference also over THI. This is identical to static GWP and only adds time detail (Ventura & Feraille Eq. 5).
- (b) Fixed calendar endpoint DO/TOD/AT (L2010, Kendall TAWP, RE2020): the numerator runs over DO - t_i and the reference CO2 pulse at t = 0 over DO. Later emissions are truncated and those after DO are dropped. Kendall's TAWP is L2010's cumulative result normalised by AGWP_CO2(AT).
- (c) Fixed horizon after each emission (Ventura 2022, and Ventura & Feraille Eq. 9): the numerator runs over exactly THI and the reference over t_i + THI, so the observation duration is t_i + THI.
- (d) Common endpoint at LCD + THI (François et al. 2026): every emission gets at least THI. The delay factor alpha(t_i) = int_0^{T-t_i} c / int_0^T c has closed forms for e^(-t/tau) kernels and for the CO2 kernel.
- Trade-offs: (b) favours delay and excludes post-endpoint impacts (Kendall, Breton, intergenerational equity) but keeps one calendar frame. (a) treats all emissions equally but mixes end dates. (c) and (d) satisfy Ventura's 'same THI for every substance and moment' principle. Heijungs (2026) rejects DCF-type modifications altogether and recommends the sustained-emissions literature.

4. Mapping onto the building C(T). This step is my own derivation, not from a source. The components are constants at t = 0, year cells (rate r over the study period), renewal events m_k at t_k, and the EoL residual at T_s.
- Under (b) with endpoint T_e: CRF(T_e) = sum_g [m_0 AGWP_g(T_e) + sum_k m_k AGWP_g(T_e - t_k) + r int_{T_e - T_s}^{T_e} AGWP_g(s) ds + m_EoL AGWP_g(T_e - T_s)].
- The year-cell integral has a closed form for the sum-of-exponentials kernel: int_{T-L}^{T} AGWP(s) ds = A[a0(TL - L^2/2) + sum a_i tau_i (L - tau_i e^(-T/tau_i)(e^(L/tau_i) - 1))].
- Dividing by AGWP_CO2(T_e) gives Kendall's 'CO2e today'. Under (c) the weight per event is AGWP_g(THI)/AGWP_CO2(t_k + THI).
- RE2020's linear year weight (1 - 0.00842 t_i), as estimated by Ventura & Feraille, clamped to [0, 50] years, is a calibrated linearisation of (b) with DO = 100. The corrected weights for a 150-year observation duration are 1.000 at year 0, 0.926 at 10, 0.835 at 25 and 0.721 at 50.
- Kendall's 75-year commercial building drops from 135,000 to 93,315 t CO2e under TAWP100 and to 127,591 t under TAWP500, so the effect is strongly horizon-dependent.

5. Matrices. The sources say little. Breton notes that DLCA combines the dynamic LCI and DCF 'by using a matrix approach'. He points to ESPA (a convolution-based structural path method) and to Temporalis/DYNCO2. The Brightway dynamic_characterization/bw_timex code is the practical implementation path.

6. Assumptions and limits that carry into the extension:
- Linearity, superposition and time-invariance of the IRF. These hold only for small pulses (<100 GtC per Breton) under an approximately constant background (Joos, Breton).
- A constant radiative efficiency, valid in the small-perturbation, constant-background limit (Joos). Ventura & Feraille note that no dynamic method models time-varying RE.
- The IRF depends on background and scenario: integrated IRF at 100 years is 62 yr at 389 ppm versus 66-75 yr under RCPs (Bern3D-LPJ). A time-invariant kernel therefore underestimates the persistence of late building emissions under high-emission futures.
- The fit is valid only for 0-1000 years.
- The definition of t = 0 matters: RE2020 uses construction, Heijungs finds t = 0 undefined in L2010, and Ventura & Feraille argue for the first extraction.
- Units are inconsistent across sources (Heijungs, and Breton's 'W yr m^-2' for GWI_inst).
- GWP-type dynamic metrics can fall under delay while GTP rises (François).
- The background system is usually kept static while only the foreground is dynamic.
results.open_questions:
1. Levasseur et al. 2010: full text not read (ACS 403, closed access; PolyPublie and the thesis returned 503). Unconfirmed: its exact equation numbering and notation, which IRF and RE it cites (AR4 is inferred from Heijungs), its DCF unit, its definition of t = 0, and whether its GWI uses instantaneous or cumulative DCFs. My two fetch summaries of Heijungs disagree on L2010's equation numbers.
2. Cherubini et al. 2011: full text not read. Unconfirmed: the y(t) Bern model version and coefficients, the regrowth function g(t) and its rotation-period form, the GWPbio values, and whether the GWPbio horizon is a fixed endpoint (as Breton says) or per emission.
3. IPCC AR5 8.SM and AR6 7.SM: not accessible (403). Unconfirmed: whether AR5 adopts exactly the Joos 2013 Table 5 coefficients; AR5/AR6 temperature-response parameters; AR6's CO2 RE (1.33e-5 W m^-2 ppb^-1 is known only from code) and any carbon-cycle-feedback adjustment.
4. Ventura 2022/2023: full text not read. The lower limit of the denominator in Heijungs' rendering of L2010 (Eq. 50) is unconfirmed. Ventura & Feraille integrate from 0.
5. Ventura & Feraille note: tau_1 and tau_3 are printed as '1 729' and '1 186' years (probably 172.9 and 1.186). The RE2020 slope 0.00842 per year (0.00845 in one place) is the authors' regression, not checked against the official RE2020 decree. CH4 RE is inconsistent within the note (3.4e-4 vs 3.7e-4).
6. Kendall 2012 supplementary material (TAWPv1.0 and best-fit polynomials) not read.
7. Breton Eq. 6: the bracket and scaling placement was reconstructed from garbled PDF text.
8. Time-dependent technosphere matrices (A(t), B(t)) are not formalised in these sources. A follow-up survey is needed on Beloin-Saint-Pierre et al. (ESPA), Temporalis (Cardellini et al. 2018), bw_timex, and Tiruta-Barna et al. 2016.
9. No source treats a time-varying background concentration or RE inside the convolution. A scenario-dependent kernel IRF(t, t') would break time-invariance and needs climate-model literature (e.g. Joos 2013 Sect. 4.4 RCP runs, or FaIR-type emulators).
10. Not yet consulted: Levasseur et al. 2012/2013 (J Ind Ecol, the corrected GWI_cum), Guest et al. 2013, Resch et al. 2021 (Building & Environment), Fouquet et al. 2015 and Negishi et al. 2018 (dynamic building LCA). Resch 2021 was found but only as an abstract.
